Military officers fumed about Ottawa Citizen's report on sexual assault in internal emails
Adams said she was disgusted, but not surprised, when she read the Meszaros email and saw the comments 
attributed to Desbiens.
She said the focus of the Canadian Forces isn't to help those who have been sexually assaulted; it is to make sure 
such incidents aren't reported on in the news media.
""They're pissed because they want (the Ottawa Citizen) to go away and stop reporting on this (sex assault),"" 
Adams said. ""They also want me to go away. Well, I'm not going anywhere.""
The records, released under the Access to Information Act, show Bourgon at first questioned why the Ottawa 
Citizen wanted a comment. But then the general appeared to acknowledge her earlier characterization of the 
assault had ""annoyed"" Adams.
Meszaros recommended Bourgon not talk to the newspaper. But the public affairs officer added: ""I completely 
appreciate the point of view of Ms. Adams, and feel her despair and frustration. She must have felt that the only 
way to get responses was by taking this to the media.""
Bourgon retired from the military in October 2025.
Lt.-Gen. Lise Bourgon was directly criticized by Kristen Adams.
In 2022, some Canadian Forces personnel told former Supreme Court Justice Louise Arbour that the military sees 
sexual misconduct as a public relations problem( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/defence-
watch/canadian-military-sees-sex-misconduct-as-pr-problem-that-needs-to-be-managed-former-soldiers-say ) that 
needs to be managed to avoid negative media coverage rather than a serious issue to actually be dealt with. Arbour 
received those comments as part of her review on military sexual misconduct.
The CFMWS provides various programs and services for the military.
In a May 10, 2023 letter, the CFMWS told Adams she should have realized she could have faced( 
https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/defence-watch/canadian-forces-worker-sexually-assaulted-at-nato-base-
told-she-should-have-realized-such-risks-existed-documents ) such an incident or other risks when she signed on 
for the job, according to documents obtained earlier by the Citizen.
CFMWS Chief Executive Officer Ian Poulter did issue an apology to all his staff for the way the incident was 
handled, although he excluded Adams.
Department of National Defence records revealed why Poulter never sent Adams an apology, even though one was 
written up; those documents noted DND and CFMWS didn't want the mea culpa reported in the Ottawa Citizen. 
""Because the story was unfolding in the pages of the Ottawa Citizen, we did not want to correspond with Ms. 
Adams in writing because we didn't want to perpetuate that cycle,"" DND officials wrote in one of the records.
Poulter, a retired Canadian Forces major general, has declined to be interviewed by the Ottawa Citizen.
The DND records indicate that rather than helping Adams, military and department officials were more concerned( 
https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/defence-watch/watchdog-canadian-military-sexual-assault-investigation ) 
about whether other news media outlets would follow the Citizen coverage and report on the sexual assault.
Eyre's then chief of staff, Brig. Gen. Brendan Cook, warned Poulter in an Oct. 25, 2023, email that ""Ms. Adams is 
likely to be coming back with more media coverage.""
Cook also raised concerns that the office of Anita Anand, then the defence minister, could take an interest in the 
matter. ""Of note, we recently got some pressure from MNDO (Minister National Defence Office) about the recent 
internal message to CFWMS staff that was cited in the press for not apologizing to Ms. Adams,"" Cook wrote to 
Poulter in an email.

The documents also showed that some CFMWS managers belittled Adams and claimed the attack never 
happened, despite police records to the contrary.
The federal government has now reached a settlement with Adams( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-
service/defence-watch/worker-sexually-assaulted-military-latvia-settlement-secret ), but the details remain secret. 
Under the agreement, Adams cannot discuss the CFMWS.
But in an article published before the agreement was put in place, Adams alleged the CFMWS failed to properly 
respond to the attack or to provide her with help. She stated at that time she believed the Canadian military was 
trying to sweep the assault under the rug because they didn't want to cause any embarrassment for the Canadian 
Armed Forces' high-profile mission in Latvia.

A veteran Montreal technology entrepreneur has acknowledged visiting Jeffrey Epstein on the financier's Caribbean 
island while raising money for a startup after newly released U.S. government files detailed years of contact 
between the two men.
Austin Hill, a co-founder and former chief executive of Montreal-based cryptocurrency firm Blockstream, said he 
met Epstein on the financier's island in April 2014 for a business meeting with colleagues and that the group stayed 
off-island and met him outdoors during the day.
Hill also confirmed that Epstein ended up indirectly investing US$500,000 in the company through a venture fund.
The relationship is documented in a trove of some three million files released last week by the U.S. Department of 
Justice pertaining to the deceased financier, a convicted sex offender who had been awaiting trial on charges of sex 
trafficking of minors. The material shows correspondence from 2014 to 2018, including discussions about bitcoin, 
government regulation and potential investments, along with several in-person meetings.
Hill said his interactions with Epstein were related to business or technology, adding that he regretted ""any 
association"" and ""unequivocally"" condemned Epstein's crimes.
The newly released files have brought renewed scrutiny over how Epstein continued to mingle among the elite 
financial, technological and academic circles years after his 2008 conviction for soliciting a minor for prostitution.
Much of that attention has focused on Epstein's ties to U.S. President Donald Trump, prominent American 
businessmen and British royalty. The records, however, show that his network extended into Canada.
Emails from April 2014 place Hill and colleagues at a Ritz-Carlton in St. Thomas, co-ordinating daily visits to 
Epstein's nearby island, Little St. James. Prosecutors and survivors have identified the island as a site where 
Epstein trafficked and sexually abused underage girls.
The emails do not allege any wrongdoing by Hill or his colleagues.
Epstein's investment, which the emails show Hill discussing directly with him, was made through a fund managed 
by Joi Ito, then director of the MIT Media Lab.

""Therefore, no separate vetting was conducted on him beyond relying on professional introductions and his 
reputation on Wall Street,"" Hill said.
He added that the investment represented less than three per cent of Blockstream's capitalization at the time and 
was divested in early 2015 because of ""an unrelated conflict of interest between MIT, Joi Ito and Blockstream.""
In a separate statement, Blockstream's co-founder and current chief executive, Adam Back, said the company has 
""no direct or indirect financial connection with Jeffrey Epstein, or his estate.""
The emails show Back, too, visited the island.
Hill, now in his 50s, has been a long-standing figure in Canada's technology sector, having built much of his career 
in Montreal.
Before Blockstream, he co-founded TotalNet, one of the country's early internet service providers. That company,

The emails show Hill first contacted Epstein in March 2014, introducing himself as working on ""global finance

Hill said his interactions with Epstein were related to fundraising for Blockstream and ""were initiated at the request

Both men were attending the TED conference in Vancouver at the time.
Subsequent correspondence suggests they met at a Fairmont hotel where Epstein was staying.
In one message, with the sender's name redacted, Hill was told how to identify Epstein. When Hill arrived, Epstein 
replied that he was ""with two pretty girls.""
Hill later followed up after their meeting to say he wanted to continue the conversation.
""Ps.,"" he added. ""Yes they were pretty :).""
The two men remained in contact, which ultimately led Hill to visit Epstein's New York City townhouse. Epstein also 
nearly travelled to Montreal to visit Hill on at least two occasions. However, the emails suggest those plans fell

On one planned trip to Montreal in 2014, as part of a stopover back to the U.S., Epstein was set to stay at the Ritz-
Carlton and see comedian Bobby Slayton's Nasty Show at the Just for Laughs festival.
Their communication tapered off after 2015. Around that time, Hill also stepped down from his executive role at 
Blockstream. The company said the reason for Hill's departure was so he could pursue other opportunities.
After that period, Hill said he had ""limited and sporadic contact with Epstein on technology-related topics.""
The emails show how their exchanges picked up again in 2017, focusing on cryptocurrency regulation and 
government policy.
In one message, Hill wrote that he and others were attempting to persuade then-prime minister Justin Trudeau 
and provincial governments to move first on cryptocurrency regulation and establish what he described as a safe 
framework.
Epstein discussed sending Hill $75,000, asking that the payment be itemized because it exceeded $25,000.

More than 400 RCMP members faced misconduct allegations in 2024, with five per cent of cases leading to 
dismissal, according to a report( https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2026/grc-rcmp/PS61-43-2024-
eng.pdf ) released by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in late January( https://rcmp.ca/en/corporate-
information/publications-and-manuals/summary-report-management-rcmp-conduct-process-2024 ).
The principal findings, say the RCMP, show that: less than two per cent of all members were involved in the 
conduct process; ""discreditable conduct"" remains the most reported contravention; and there is a trend towards 
more serious disciplinary outcomes.
It should be noted that RCMP members include police officers and civilian members who support police operations. 
The Code of Conduct applies to both, on- and off-duty, within and outside of Canada.
In 2024, 443 conduct files were opened, ""marking a return to a consistent level compared to the pandemic years,"" 
according to the report. The numbers dipped between 2021 and 2023, when the RCMP's case counts dropped.
Ultimately, in 2024, there were 408 RCMP members across all ranks alleged to have contravened the police 
service's Code of Conduct. (There are 21,641 RCMP members.)
Conduct allegations were proportional to the number of any rank in the service. For example, constables 
represented 54 per cent of the overall membership but accounted for 61 per cent of misconduct cases, a slight 
over-representation relative to their share of the force. Corporals (17 per cent), sergeants (10 per cent), and staff 
sergeants (4 per cent) each accounted for a proportion of misconduct cases directly in line with their share of the 
membership. Members with the rank of inspectors and above represented 4 per cent of the misconduct case 
compared to 3 per cent of the workforce, a slight over-representation.
Civilian members accounted for only 3 per cent of the misconduct cases, while comprising 12 per cent of the 
membership.
In 2024, discreditable conduct continued to represent the largest number of allegations. According to the report, that 
encompasses a wide range of behaviours. Some examples include improper posts on social media, sexual 
misconduct, and Criminal Code offences. (Full details about these allegations were not provided in the report. Nor 
were specific details provided about any other allegations set out in it.)

Frequently cited allegations, aside from discreditable conduct, included improper use of equipment, diligence in aid, 
conflict of interest, and failure to give and carry out lawful orders and direction. Allegations related to use of force, 
abuse of authority, and unauthorized access or use of information rounded out the top 10, says the RCMP.
Conduct authorities or boards (the latter involves lawyers) are responsible for initiating an investigation and 
determining if a member's conduct has amounted to a contravention of the Code of Conduct. If it has, they impose 
conduct measures that ""are appropriate to the nature and circumstances of the contravention.""
Measures to deal with the conduct ""show a marked shift compared to previous years,"" according to the RCMP 
report. ""While remedial measures decreased significantly from 51 per cent in 2023 to 29 per cent in 2024, corrective 
(measures) rose to 42 per cent. More notable is the increase in the serious measures (24 per cent in 2024 versus 
14 per cent in 2023) and dismissals (5 per cent in 2024 versus 1 per cent in 2023).""
This shows a trend toward ""more serious disciplinary outcomes, aligning with the RCMP's emphasis on 
accountability and proportionate responses to misconduct,"" states the report.
Compared to the two years prior, the number of demotions more than doubled in 2024. Demotion as a disciplinary 
measure holds members accountable while preserving the opportunity for rehabilitation and continued service.
Meanwhile, ""interim administrative steps"" may be taken while a member is the subject of conduct proceedings. 
They are designed to protect the well-being of employees and the integrity of the RCMP, pending the outcome of 
the Code of Conduct investigation. Some examples include stoppage of pay and allowances (which, according to 
the report, ""remains rare""), suspension with pay (applied in 105 cases in 2024, a 47 per cent increase over the 
previous years) and temporary reassignment (the most frequently used measure, averaging 103 cases annually).
These disciplinary process reports derive from a 2008 Minister of Public Safety directive requiring the RCMP to 
provide annual data.

Suzanne Craig, who was recently appointed to the role of Integrity Commissioner for the Town of Essex, took the 
time to introduce herself to Council at the December 1 meeting.
At the previous meeting, Council appointed Craig to the role, after accepting the resignation of former Integrity 
Commissioner, Bruce Elman, which was effective November 30.
Craig’s appointment is effective from December 1, 2025 to November 30, 2027. There will be two options to extend 
for an additional two-years each extension. That means if Council approves the extensions in the future, she could 
remain in this role for up to six-years.
Craig thanked Council for giving her the opportunity to serve as Integrity Commissioner, and noted she plans to visit 
the area in-person to meet with everyone. She resides in Toronto. 
“I believe the Code of Conduct belongs to Council,” Craig said. “It is a living document. It doesn’t rest forever, and it 
changes over time.”
That can be based on legislative changes, because there has been a significant code complaint, or to address best 
practices that come out of court, Craig added.
“I am an ethics resource. One of my duties... is to be an independent resource to Council,” she said, noting the role 
holder can be an important resource for ethical expertise.
An Integrity Commissioner provides significant profile to ethical issues inside government, “and sends an important 
message to your constituents about your commitment to ethical governance,” Craig added.
From time-to-time, she will develop info bulletins to guide Council and assist residents in understanding Council’s 
roles and responsibilities.
In her role, she will also conduct investigations based on complaints that believe an ethical violation has taken 
place. 

Page 2 of 3
New Integrity Commissioner Suzanne Craig introduces herself to Essex Council
“I see that as one of the less important roles and duties I have, because in my role as Integrity Commissioner, 
education and outreach is the most important,” Craig explained.
She intends to clarify to Council the rules of its Code of Conduct.
To ensure transparency in the work she does, she publishes an annual periodic report that sets out what she has 
done, outlines the number of code complaints she received, identifies if they were formal or informal, and if they 
have been settled, dismissed, or brought to Council’s attention. She also outlines any issues she believes are 
important to Council regarding matters that came to her office.
She also publishes the expenses of her office.
As of 2019, Craig noted Integrity Commissioners can receive an application to see if a Council member has 
breached the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act. In the case it is believed a member has breached that, the 
enforcement goes through the courts, Craig added.
“I believe that an Integrity Commissioner is an independent officer, who operates at arm’s length of Council. But 
must keep present that she reports to Council. I report to you and I work for you on behalf of the public interest,” 
Craig said.
She is a lawyer by training, public servant by vocation, and collaborates with a group of professionals who work with 
her to provide legal advice and research to her consultancy.
While many may see the role of an Integrity Commissioner as punitive and only about investigating code complaints 
and recommending penalties, Craig views her role as “facilitating a clear understanding of what the Code is, but 
also what the Code is not. So, that you, your staff, and the public see the code, and my role as the facilitator, to help 
you understand your roles and responsibilities, and not an enabler of weaponizing the Code.” 
In answering Councillor Kim Verbeek’s question if any ongoing issues that were being handled by the previous 
Integrity Commissioner would be passed on to her, Craig noted if there is an outstanding matter she will work with 
the outgoing Integrity Commissioner or Town staff. She does not believe there are, and said there will be a 
seamless transition.
Joe Malandruccolo, Director of Legal and Legislative Services, noted the previous Integrity Commissioner is to 
transfer any ongoing matters onto the new role holder. He will contact Elman and ensure that is coordinated if there 
are.

On January 23, news broke of sexual misconduct charges being laid against a former teacher in the Hanover 
School Division—specifically, Braeden Martens, who taught at the Steinbach Regional Secondary School (SRSS). 
According to the Steinbach RCMP, Martens faces charges of luring a child under the age of 16 and an invitation to 
sexual touching. These incidents allegedly took place between September 2023 and January 2025.
The school division promptly removed him from his teaching position when the allegations first surfaced in early 
2025, although an entire year passed before details were released to the public.
As the story made headlines in the past few weeks, it wasn’t just Martens facing public scrutiny. HSD also came 
under the microscope.
According to reporting in the Winnipeg Free Press, there was more to the story than accusations of child sexual 
abuse. Their article suggested that Martens had been allowed to teach at the SRSS without proof of provincial 
certification.
The Free Press reported that Martens’s name never appeared on the Manitoba Teacher Professional Conduct 
Registry. This provincial database, created one year ago, is intended to provide the public with a transparent look at 
teacher suspensions and charges of misconduct.
Every certified teacher in Manitoba is supposed to appear on this registry, whether or not they hold a clean 
teaching record. Since Martens does not appear on the list, his alleged misconduct could not be reported on it.
Three days after the Free Press article was published, HSD offered an official response.
“In the interest of transparency and maintaining public trust, Hanover School Division is issuing this statement to 
clarify inaccuracies, including statements in the article that were uninformed and/or patently false.”
Rebutting what they believed were insinuations that Martens was never authorized to teach at all, HSD clarified that 
they applied for, and received from the province, four separate Limited Teaching Permits (LTP) over the years. This 
means that Martens was legally eligible to teach at the SRSS during those terms. HSD also confirmed that each 
permit was accompanied by the required child abuse registry check and criminal record check.

By the fall of 2024, HSD did not apply for a fifth LTP, as they believed Martens was waiting on his permanent 
teaching certification from the province.
Four months later, he was removed from his teaching position at the SRSS following allegations of sexual 
misconduct.
For those four months, it would appear that Martens was indeed practicing without a license. The Citizen reached 
out to the HSD for an explanation.
“The individual was transitioning from a Limited Teaching Permit—valid with all required safety clearances as of 
June 2024—to teacher certification,” says HSD superintendent Joe Thiessen. “Unlike Limited Teaching Permits, 
which are submitted by the division, teacher certification applications are initiated by the applicant through the 
Professional Certification Unit. In this case, the application was not submitted during the referenced period [of] fall 
2024.”
Manitoba’s Minister of Education, Tracy Schmidt, also responded to the Free Press’s article.
“The safety and well-being of students is our government’s highest priority,” Schmidt says. “Parents deserve full 
confidence that every teacher working in our schools is properly vetted and authorized to be in the classroom.” 
Teaching Permits and Certification 
To work as a Kindergarten to Grade 12 teacher in Manitoba, one must be registered through the province as either 
a professional certified teacher, a provisional professional teacher, or a short-term limited teacher.
Obtaining permanent professional status requires a minimum of a bachelor’s degree in education from a locally 
recognized university.
A three-year provisional license can be obtained for those working towards their professional certification.
Finally, a Limited Teaching Permit allows non-certified instructors to work in specific schools for one term at a time. 
This permit can be renewed repeatedly, at the province’s discretion.
“Individuals granted an LTP do not have their teaching experience recognized by Manitoba Education and Early 
Childhood Learning,” the provincial LTP application states. “A LTP may be granted in cases where the school is 
able to provide evidence demonstrating efforts to recruit and hire a Manitoba certified teacher have occurred but 
have not been successful.”
According to HSD, Martens worked at the SRSS for four terms under a legitimate LTP permit and with security 
documents that checked out.
Martens graduated as a Red Seal electrician from RRC Polytech’s Technical Vocational program in 2024. By 
summer of that year, his LTP permit had expired and was not renewed by the school division.
The employment of LTP teachers is common in Manitoba, especially since the years of the COVID-19 pandemic.
According to the Free Press, there are nearly 900 LTP educators in Manitoba’s grade schools this school year 
alone, more than twice the number who were teaching in this province ten years ago. 
Provincial Role 
Unfortunately, HSD’s explanation as to why Martens was on their payroll without official certification during the fall 
and winter of 2024 is vague. Was it an administrative lapse or did the division believe Martens’ official paperwork 
was imminent?
According to a provincial spokesperson, it can take anywhere between two to 12 weeks to process documents of 
certification.

“Processing times vary based on factors such as the volume of applications in queue and the applicant’s academic 
credentials,” the spokesperson says.
Perhaps a more pointed question should arise: what is the province’s responsibility in this?
While Minister Schmidt promises to make student safety and well-being a top priority, it’s not a provincial 
requirement for LTP educators to be listed on their teacher professional conduct registry. The registry includes only 
the names of professional certified teachers and authorized clinicians.
So whether Martens was operating under a legitimate LTP license or no license at all, his name would never have 
been found there. That is not the fault of the HSD.
“Our government is acting immediately and decisively to close gaps, reinforce oversight, and ensure that every 
student in Manitoba is protected,” Schmidt states.
For reassurances, The Citizen reached out to Schmidt’s office to ask whether the professional conduct registry 
would soon include every person who holds a position in Manitoba’s public school system, including LTP 
educators. No quotable response was offered.
Instead the minister is focused on ensuring that school divisions review their teacher certifications and the 
background checks that accompany them. This is nothing new. It’s simply a reminder for divisions to be vigilant in 
their compliance to existing law.
Manitoba’s school divisions are to report back to the province by March. 
Criminal Checks and Abuse Registries 
According to RCMP Media Relations Officer Corporal Melanie Roussel, for a small fee individuals can request 
documentation from the police to verify their criminal background or lack thereof. This is known as a criminal record 
check. Anyone can request one for themselves, and an employer can ask to see a copy. However, employers may 
not obtain from the police a criminal record check on behalf of any employee.
Indications of past criminal activity are limited to actual convictions and don’t typically reflect allegations or charges. 
A person can function in society for a long time with allegations that haven’t yet been proven in court.
“[A person] won’t have a criminal record if there’s no conviction,” Roussel says. “It can take years before they get a 
conviction. They get a trial and the trial can be set up in a year or more from now.”
The province has another tool, called the child abuse registry. A child protection committee determines who earns a 
place on that registry.
Roussel says that she sat on such a committee for a time, representing law enforcement. Also on the committee 
were doctors, social workers, and other professionals. Together they reviewed charges to decide whether 
individuals should be listed.
According to Roussel, it’s unlikely that Martens’s name will appear on the child abuse registry until he is formally 
convicted of a crime in a court of law, a process that could take years, if it ever happens.
What about teachers who are guilty of sexual misconduct that goes unreported by their victims? Until someone 
has the courage to step forward—and for a child, it takes an enormous amount of courage—such a teacher’s name 
would appear on no registries for either employers or the public to see. Their registry checks would come back 
clean.

HALIFAX - Nova Scotia’s largest utility is responding to a stinging letter from Premier Tim Houston by insisting it 
hasn't broken any laws.
The statement came after Houston sent a letter to the chair of the energy board, calling for an investigation into how 
the private utility has handled a cyberattack and saying residents should not be responsible for paying for Nova 
Scotia Power's failures.
Nova Scotia Power, a subsidiary of Halifax-based Emera Inc., has said the personal and financial data belonging 
to 280,000 ratepayers was accessed by an unauthorized party as early as March 19. Since then, the utility has said 
it can no longer rely on remote meter readings and as a result is estimating electricity consumption for some 
customers' billing.
In response, Houston said customers have been dealing with inflated bills, consecutive charges within short 
periods, and a lack of communication about billing adjustments. 
“It’s not lost on me or the board that knowingly overbilling would constitute regulatory fraud and misreporting 
revenue to the markets is a form of securities fraud,” Houston said in his letter.
In an emailed statement Wednesday night, a Nova Scotia Power spokesperson said the utility is complying with all 
securities and regulatory laws, and dismisses any suggestion to the contrary.
""In spite of everything that has transpired since the initial cyberattack we are working very hard to restore all of our 
system functionality. We understand and are sorry for the frustration that our customers are experiencing,"" 
Jacqueline Foster said.
Foster said that meters have not been able to send usage information back to their billing system since the 
cyberattack. She said this was why the utility estimates usage on many customer bills. To date, she added that staff 
have been able to visit homes and manually record meters for 75 per cent of customers.
""We are committed to rebuilding trust and will do that by supporting our customers and fixing it when we make a 
mistake,"" she added.

TORONTO - The Ontario government has filed a lawsuit against a company it contracted to run a student mental 
health program, alleging fraudulent misrepresentation and seeking to recoup more than $25 million in public money.
Ontario alleges Keel Digital Solutions, through its subsidiary Get A-Head Inc., inflated the number of counselling 
sessions it reported delivering to students, resulting in overpayments of millions of dollars. The company vigorously 
denies the allegations.
Between 2022 and 2025, the company ""provided false and misleading quarterly reports of their corporate 
performance measures,"" which were the basis for its payments, the government alleged in its lawsuit.
""The false reports caused the Crown to pay the corporate defendants millions of dollars that they otherwise would 
not have been paid,"" alleged the claim, which was filed in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice on Wednesday.
The company said it would be filing a counterclaim.
""The government’s lawsuit against Keel Digital Solutions is deeply flawed, built on misstatements and outright 
inaccuracies,"" chief operating officer Jay Fischbach wrote Friday in a statement. 
""Keel Digital has never been involved in any fraudulent activity, and we fully expect the government of Ontario to 
be compelled to retract its claims, apologize, and answer for the recklessness and malice that drove this case.""
Keel Digital Solutions was closely scrutinized during the fall sitting of the legislature as one of the recipients of the 
Ministry of Labour's $2.5-billion Skills Development Fund, a program the auditor general has found was not fair or 
transparent and doled out money to applicants ranked low by bureaucrats. 
Labour Minister David Piccini came under sustained fire from opposition parties calling for his resignation, 
particularly since media reports said one of Keel's lobbyists is a close friend of Piccini's.
That heat only increased after the government announced it had referred the results of an audit on Keel's funding 
from the Ministry of Colleges and Universities to the Ontario Provincial Police, citing concerns dating back to 2023.

Critics questioned why the Ministry of Labour gave Keel $7.5 million in skills development funding for a first 
responder mental health program even after an audit of their student funding had raised concerns within a different 
ministry.
Piccini has said Keel Digital Solutions is one of the applicants that bureaucrats had ranked low but the ministry 
decided to fund. He has defended the practice of granting funding to low-scoring applications, saying that's done 
when they align with government priorities.
Ontario Provincial Police announced last month that they had launched an investigation into Keel's student mental 
health funding.
Liberal parliamentary leader John Fraser said the government's lawsuit seems self-serving, given that the police are 
already on the matter.
""This legal action appears designed to distract from the deeper and far more troubling problems at the heart of the 
Skills Development Fund,"" he wrote in a statement.
""Doug Ford now wants Ontarians to believe his government was swindled. They were not swindled. They were 
caught.""
In the province's lawsuit, Ontario alleges the company filed estimated expenses as opposed to actual expenses, 
failed to report unspent funds and interest earned, and overstated the metrics upon which its funding was based.
Get A-Head reported sessions providing counselling to people other than students as well as training mock 
sessions as student mental health sessions, the province alleges. It also reported the time spent by a counsellor, 
supervisor and student in one session as three separate sessions, the lawsuit alleges.
""(The company's) 2022-2023 final report claimed 42,556 eligible sessions between March 31, 2022 and March 30, 
2023,"" the government wrote in its lawsuit. 
""In actual fact, the Crown has learned that there were only 3,529 unique sessions of any duration during that 
period.""
The province also alleges several executives at the company ""directed, facilitated, and then tried to cover up the 
corporate defendants' false reports"" given to the ministry.
None of the allegations have been tested in court.
The company has previously said it has complied with all laws and contractual obligations and looks forward to an 
apology from the government at the end of the police probe.
Premier Doug Ford and Piccini have repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and both have said they remain committed 
to the Skills Development Fund.
Ontario's integrity commissioner, Cathryn Motherwell, has also launched an ethics investigation into Piccini's 
dealings with that fund.
Media reports have said that some beneficiaries of the fund are unions that endorsed the Progressive 
Conservatives in elections and people who have donated to the party.
The auditor general also found that more than 60 of the lower-scoring fund applicants were approved after they 
hired a lobbyist, which had the opposition crying foul over what they called preferential treatment.
The Skills Development Fund gives money to organizations for projects that help hire, train or retrain workers. The 
province says they've so far trained about 700,000 people and of those, 100,000 people found jobs within 60 days 
of completing the program.

QUEBEC - There is no evidence that Pablo Rodriguez ""participated in or was informed"" in any way of allegedly 
dubious fundraising tactics during his 2025 Quebec Liberal leadership campaign, a retired Superior Court judge 
has concluded.
And after weeks of investigating, Jacques Fournier says there is no way to verify the authenticity or falseness of a 
series of text messages, allegedly between Liberal supporters, suggesting votes for Rodriguez were being 
purchased for the price of a ""brownie"" (slang for a $100 bill).
Le Journal de Montréal broke the story on Nov. 19( https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2025/11/19/il-faut-encore-
payer-pour-que-le-monde-vote-pablo-des-textos-troublants-derriere-la-crise-au-plq ), based on phone text 
messages it had obtained. The Liberals enlisted Fournier to independently investigate.
If anything, Fournier says in his 40-page report handed to the Liberals Wednesday, there is clear evidence the text 
messages are ""only a montage"" cobbled together from other original messages.
None of the texts are clearly dated, so there is no time frame on when they were sent, and there is no way to 
establish their origin, the judge says.
But Fournier also recognizes it is not possible for him to conclude that the texts were false or fabricated by the 
sources used by Le Journal de Montréal, because he did not have access to the entire messages.
As a result, he says he cannot conclude whether someone bought votes or not.
""It is clearly impossible to know the source of something if it did not exist,"" he says.
One thing he does conclude: Rodriguez knew nothing.
""Nothing indicates (Rodriguez) participated or was informed of any (fundraising) irregularities before having 
knowledge of the (Journal de Montréal) article Nov. 19, 2025,"" Fournier concludes in his report, which was released 
to the media.
""None of the revelations that appeared in the newspaper implicate him directly.""

snowballed into a question of confidence, has always denied any knowledge of what may have been going on(

An immigrant pharmacist whose Canadian citizenship was revoked in November 2024, a decade after officials first 
suspected she hadn't met the requirements, has seen that decision set aside and revocation proceedings 
permanently stayed by a Federal Court judge, who criticized officials for waiting so long to act on the allegations of 
""false re -p resentation, fraud, or knowingly concealing material circumstances.""
Nermine Magdi Ibrahim, who became a permanent resident in July 2003 and subsequently a Canadian citizen in 
October 2007, applied to the Federal Court for a judicial review of the revocation proceedings.
Immigration officials were not ""concerned about the impact of the delay on (Ibrahim's) ability to defend her case, nor 
(her) well-established ties to Canada as reasons for granting her special relief,"" Justice Avvy Yao-Yao Go wrote in 
a recent decision out of Toronto.
""In short, the unfairness with which the applicant was treated, coupled with the unfairness in the proceedings 
caused by the delay, calls into question the integrity of the justice system if the court allows the proceedings to 
continue under these circumstances."" In her citizenship application, Ibrahim ""declared 166 days of absences from 
Canada during her relevant residency period from July 9, 2003 to February 18, 2007,"" Go said.
Ibrahim's citizenship was initially flagged for investigation in 2014; it was completed that same year.
The Canada Border Services Agency had ""received a tip about companies operating citizenship fraud schemes 
with (Ibrahim's) husband's name appearing as one of the clients who used these services to simulate his residence 
in Canada,"" said the Federal Court decision, dated Dec. 19.
The CBSA referred this information to the immigration minister for further investigation.
""During its investigation, the case management branch ... found (Ibrahim's) LinkedIn profile which suggested that 
she was continuously employed as a Medical Delegate with Nestlé Infant Nutrition in Kuwait from June 2002 to 
June 2009,"" Go said.
""On July 23, 2014, an analyst of the Immigration Section at the Canadian Embassy in Abu Dhabi, United Arab 
Emirates verified her continuous employment with the employer.""

says
It wasn't until 2023 when Canadian immigration authorities advised Ibrahim of the potential revocation proceedings 
and offered her an opportunity to respond.
They argued ""that the delay was not unreasonable considering this case was part of a large-scale investigation 
involving 300 other individuals.""
The judge wasn't buying it: ""Based on the record before me, I find that the minister has not provided any 
justification for the delay,"" Go said.
To become a Canadian citizen, permanent residents need to have lived in Canada for three out of the last five 
years.
In September 2023, immigration officials wrote to Ibrahim indicating she ""may have misrepresented herself during 
the citizenship process and that (she) may have failed to disclose some of her absences from Canada during the 
four years immediately before the date of her citizenship application,"" said the decision.
She was given 30 days ""to make written submissions regarding the length of time she spent in Canada before 
acquiring citizenship and her ties to Canada since becoming a citizen,"" it said.
Ibrahim responded on Sept. 21, 2023, with a letter requesting ""more details about alleged absences and stated that 
she has integrated well into Canadian society as shown in her successfully becoming licensed as a pharmacist, 
being a partner of two pharmacies, and owning property,"" said the decision ""She also argued that the revocation 
would result in severe hardship and added that all her points can be substantiated with supporting documents upon 
request.""
On May 9, 2024, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) notified Ibrahim it was revoking her 
citizenship. It noted her employment with Nestlé in Kuwait among the reasons for alleging that she ""may have 
obtained citizenship by misrepresentation.""
Ibrahim responded ""that her LinkedIn Profile is not of a factual nature and does not include any leaves taken.""
She ""also explained that she was pregnant with her daughter during the relevant period, and that Nestlé had a 
relatively flexible maternity leave policy that enabled her to stay in Canada for the duration of her pregnancy and 
throughout the breastfeeding period until her daughter was two years old.""
Ibrahim argued the immigration minister put the onus on her to prove ""she was a resident in Canada when she has 
no such obligation.""
Immigration officials, she said, did not make the decision to revoke her Canadian citizenship ""based on any 
evidence of misrepresentation.""
The judge found the long delay in dealing with Ibrahim's case constituted ""an abuse of process.""
Go also found ""the integrity of the justice system has been prejudiced as a result.""

Doug Ford faces a growing political problem with a seemingly obvious solution.
That problem is David Piccini, Ontario's embattled minister of labour.
Day by day Piccini sinks deeper into the muck, whence he greased the wheels of the premier's grimy re-election 
machine. He scooped that muck out of the government's so-called Skills Development Fund, which amounted to a 
slush fund - in some cases doling out public money to friendly labour unions that could be counted on to endorse 
the Progressive Conservative government in last February's campaign.
Now, the cheques have come to roost.
Ontario's auditor general has sifted the slush and sniffed the cash. Her audit's bottom line is that the minister's 
math made no sense.
Mysteriously, recent multimillion-dollar submissions with low ratings still merited his signature for approval - more, 
on average, then high-rated applicants. In Piccini's peculiar judgment, it seemed prudent to override the best advice 
of non-partisan civil servants for the worst kind of hyperpartisan vote-buying.
Amid the stench, the opposition smells blood. They are calling for Piccini's head, berating him as a buffoon.
Will Ford decapitate his cabinet minister to save his own skin? Be careful what you wish for, for a buffoon can be a 
buffer.
Ultimately, this is a problem of the premier's own making.
Typically, when you fire the fall guy, the problem fades away. But in Ford's case, his fingerprints are all over the 
skills development and slush dissemination fund.
That's why the premier is loath to let him go. Piccini is more useful as a foil than a fall guy - a convenient target 
(and distraction) for opposition taunts and torments while he watches from a safe distance.
A run-of-the-mill minister, Piccini ran the slush fund but didn't own it. It was the orphaned brainchild of the premier.
Page 2 of 3
Picinni is a better buffer than fall guy Ford is in no hurry to fire hapless labour minister, a convenient distraction 
for premier's critics
But the minister adopted it as his own. As the auditor discovered, Piccini - who cut his teeth as a political aide and 
knows how to sideline the bureaucracy - systematically disregarded the ratings of his ministry's civil servants, 
imposing his own political priorities over their fiscal prudence.
The result, the auditor concluded in a special report last month, was that Piccini's ministry handed out public money 
from the $2.5 billion fund to at least 64 organizations in a manner she deemed was not ""fair, transparent or 
accountable.""
Under fire after the fact, Piccini fends off criticism daily in the legislature by insisting he could see what civil servants 
couldn't fathom - the hidden talents of applicants, the unseen potential of favoured trade unions (whose fidelity 
Ford's Tories could be counted on), the presumed trustworthiness of unproven organizations. Tens of millions of 
dollars have been disbursed on the say-so of a politicized Piccini, empowered by a populist premier in pursuit of 
ever more popularity.
Tempting as it is to decry this as debased, it is par for the course. Every party in power is prone to shovelling cash 
out the door - whether from slush funds or the general treasury - passing the buck from elected governments to 
unelected, unaccountable entities who are entrusted with massive amounts of public money without public scrutiny.
The Ford government isn't the first to give away the store, if not always for political purposes. Remember the 
notorious e-Health and ORNGE scandals that beset previous Liberal governments?
When the provincial auditor poked into Piccini's pig in a poke, her agenda wasn't to expose partisan impropriety but 
governmental incompetence. She had good reason to hypothesize that the downstream problem would be lack of 
fiscal transparency by the building trades and other recipients.
Indeed, the civil servants who scrutinized some of the more dubious applications repeatedly flagged the 
questionable abilities and capacities of Tory-friendly recipients (and others) to meet the high accounting standards 
required for public funding.
In opposition, the Tories frequently complained about government giveaways that amounted to corporate welfare 
for those with their hands out. Now that the shoe is on the other foot, Ford is sitting pretty in the premier's chair.
Even if you set aside any philosophical objection to government grants - corporate or labour, cultural or charitable - 
the lack of proper accountability doubtless keeps the auditor awake at night.
As for Piccini's presumed peril, he can sleep well at night even while the auditor stays up all night. For the moment, 
he is safeguarded by his status as a foil guy, not a fall guy.
Indeed, he's probably the safest minister in a cabinet populated by one too many bumblers and boondogglers for 
Ford to fire in one fell swoop. Perhaps Ford hopes to wait it out until the legislature rises early next month for its 
pre-Christmas break, or possibly the premier is biding his time before a cabinet shuffle if the scandal dies down.
The only certainty is that Ford's Tories remain focused on the politics, not the governance. Yet the root problems 
will return to haunt the premier, because at the end of the day bad government is bad politics.

When news broke this month of the Toronto Police Service corruption that ""facilitated shootings, extortions and a 
conspiracy to commit murder,"" it felt like an escalation of the long and sometimes fraught relationship between the 
city and its police force.
A difficult time two years ago came to mind. Then, as now, it was municipal budget season and the police were 
asking for another substantial increase. As public debate swirled with a new mayor in power, the police mounted a 
bully campaign that the Star's editorial board called ""emotional blackmail."" Chief Myron Demkiw insinuated calamity 
would ensue if they didn't get what they demanded.
More inflammatory was an ad campaign run by the Toronto Police Association (TPA) that used carjacking images 
with a man pointing a gun at a driver while pulling him out of his vehicle.
Demkiw, along with Chief Jim MacSween and Deputy Chief Ryan Hogan from York Region, held a news 
conference Feb. 5 to discuss the investigation into corruption allegations that include links to shootings across the 
city, tow truck violence and even a conspiracy to murder a corrections officer. During the event, each chief 
conspicuously wore an identical flak jacket, as if ready for battle. But with whom, you might ask?
News conferences are not out in public and usually only attended by media and police officers. Looking at other 
photos of Demkiw in similar situations or actually in public, he's often just in shirt sleeves or a jacket, making the 
choice to wear body armour at this particular moment of contrition baffling.
TPA ads feel hypocritical now, too, considering that the activity Toronto police are accused of is not so different 
from what was meant to frighten Torontonians into supporting the budget increase two years ago.
Just the perception of gun violence can create great fear (it's why the TPA used it) so these very real allegations 
escalate this scandal high above others. There are even charges of uniform trafficking, creating another fear that 
police we meet day to day aren't who they appear to be.
So here we are, with Toronto's biggest police scandal in decades - one that undermines whatever level of trust 
people have in the police. The social contract of policing rests on trust.
While numerous groups within Toronto have had serious issues trusting police historically, the current scandal will 
have a much wider blast radius.
Page 2 of 3
Police corruption scandal demands these three actions
Here are three things that need to happen - soon:
The investigation must be open, transparent and entirely public
So often, police matters are dealt with internally, with little public scrutiny. Not this time. Ontario's Inspector General 
said last week he's going to review all 45 police forces across the province in the wake of this scandal.
A good start, but already there's opposition. The TPA submitted a letter to the Inspector General ""expressing 
serious concern"" over what might be an ""overly broad review."" That is exactly the kind of review needed, and the 
TPA's combativeness can be taken as a sign of how rank and file officers might co-operate with investigations.
Some, including Premier Doug Ford, have used variations of the ""just a few bad apples"" bromide. To extend this 
tired metaphor, if the rest of the apples appear hostile to an investigation, what should the public think about the 
whole bushel? Rot spreads.
There should be zero tolerance of police intimidation of civilian oversight and budget deliberations
The campaign two years ago seems to have worked, as there's been little push back since. The scandal should 
have been an opportunity to debate this year's $94-million budget increase. As my colleague Matt Elliot wrote last 
week, police are doing less and asking for more money, but no real debate occurred.
Related to this, the police board and its chair need to be far stronger and demand reform. So often they appear 
passive. Police have intimidated council in the past, as in 2000 when the TPA ran ""Operation True Blue,"" raising 
money to investigate politicians who weren't friendly to the police - and they've done the same with the police board. 
Susan Eng, the late, courageous and outspoken chair in the 1990s, was spied on by police for doing so.
The conspiracy to murder a corrections officer, along with this history of intimidation, is enough to make any public 
official, Toronto resident or member of the media pause and think about criticizing the police now.
Demkiw must resign
This happened under his watch and the public needs a sign that it's being taken seriously from top to bottom. 
Demkiw should have resigned after his comments in 2024 implying he'd have liked a different verdict for Umar 
Zameer, the man acquitted of wrongdoing in the tragic accident that saw a plainclothes police officer killed, a case 
that also involved allegations that officers colluded to incriminate Zameer (speaking of long-term systemic trust 
issues).
This is the worst kind of corruption undermining the foundations of policing. Repairing it will need a relentless, 
unflinching effort.

HALIFAX - The premier of Nova Scotia is calling for an investigation into how a major power utility has handled a 
cyberattack, saying residents should not be responsible for paying for Nova Scotia Power's failures.
Tim Houston wrote to the chair of the Nova Scotia Energy Board, saying he wants the regulator to look into the 
way the private utility has billed customers since a system breach in March.
""The cyberattack was the not the fault of Nova Scotians, yet they are bearing the financial consequences of NSP's 
(Nova Scotia Power) operational shortcomings,"" Houston said in the letter he shared on social media Wednesday.
Nova Scotia Power, a subsidiary of Halifax-based Emera Inc., has said the personal and financial data belonging 
to 280,000 ratepayers was accessed by an unauthorized party as early as March 19. Since then, the utility has said 
it can no longer rely on remote meter readings and has chosen to estimate electricity consumption for some 
customers' billing.
As a result, Houston said customers have been dealing with inflated bills, consecutive charges within short periods, 
and a lack of communication about billing adjustments. “It’s not lost on me or the board that knowingly overbilling 
would constitute regulatory fraud and misreporting revenue to the markets is a form of securities fraud,” Houston 
said in his letter.
Nova Scotia Power did not immediately return interview requests.
Wednesday morning, before Houston shared his letter, the official Opposition NDP held a press conference calling 
on Houston's government to take meaningful action to help Nova Scotians dealing with inaccurate and unaffordable 
power bills. 
Party leader Claudia Chender said that instead of helping Nova Scotians, the government has kicked 46,000 
people out of eligibility for a home-heating assistance program and reduced the one-time rebate amount of that 
program by $200. The Houston government, Chender added, has also refused the NDP's proposal to lower bills by 
10 per cent through a new rebate ""and has repeatedly refused to have government members come to committee to 
explain how they are going to make power more affordable and more reliable.""

policing.

openness, accountability, and real consequences for wrongdoing - no matter who is involved.""

A Toronto youth group is facing a $3.29-million lawsuit by the provincial government over alleged misuse of money 
from the controversial Skills Development Fund.
In a statement of claim dated Dec. 11, the Ontario government says Justice Fund Toronto and its director, Yonis 
Hassan, the not-for-profit's ""sole director, alter ego and directing mind,"" was awarded nearly $4 million by the 
Ministry of Labour in March 2023 to give ""life skills training"" for roughly 800 marginalized young people but failed to 
do so.
Filed in Ontario Superior Court, the lawsuit claims Hassan and the Justice Fund benefited from ""unjust enrichment"" 
of taxpayer dollars. 
Its allegations have not been proven in court. The Star made numerous attempts to contact Hassan, but did not 
receive a response. 
Hassan has had a media presence in recent years, including events with Noah ""40"" Shebib, a music producer and 
friend of the rapper Drake. Shebib, who previously referred to himself as a Justice Fund co-founder, is quoted, 
along with Hassan, in an August 2023 CBC story, saying Drake planned to donate $1 from every ticket sold to his 
""It's All a Blur"" tour to the group.
Hassan is the only director named on the federal corporate records for the Justice Fund. Neither Shebib nor Drake 
face any allegations and neither were named in the lawsuit.
In the 12-page statement of claim, the government alleges that Hassan and his organization ""repeatedly avoided or 
neglected"" visits from Labour Ministry staff investigating ""non-compliance"" of the funding agreement. Justice Fund 
did not file all of the required expenditure reports which, the lawsuit said, led to a government-led forensic audit that 
found ""inappropriate use"" of the SDF money.
Last summer, on July 3, the ministry demanded repayment of $3.29 million. Two weeks later, the Justice Fund filed 
articles of dissolution to shoot down operations which, the government claimed, was a ""breach of trust and 
fiduciary duties."" That action was later cancelled and the organization remains active.

statements to the ministry and scheduled visits to the ministry staff.

approved.

QUEBEC - The CAQ government moved Friday to plug a hole in the electoral code that, up until now, has made 
vote buying in party leadership races legal.
The bill comes in response to allegations( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-
rodriguez-vote-buying-allegations ) that certain Quebec Liberal Party members received ""brownies"" - or $100 bills - 
to support Pablo Rodriguez in his successful run for party leader this spring. The proposed legislation was tabled 
Friday.
The Liberals have since launched an independent investigation( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebecs-liberals-inquiry-vote-buying-allegations ) into the 
matter and Quebec's anti-corruption unit( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/upac-quebec-
liberals-vote-buying-allegations ) has interviewed witnesses.
""Before the events of these last weeks, I didn't think it was necessary to table a bill like this one,"" Democratic 
Institutions Minister Jean-François Roberge said Friday after tabling the bill.
Roberge said he had been surprised to learn cash-for-vote schemes were legal in leadership races under Quebec's 
electoral laws.
""It was a blind spot,"" Roberge said. ""I saw this problem, I wanted to fix it.""
The bill would apply both to party leadership races and riding nomination contests. It would make it illegal to either 
offer or accept ""a gift, loan, office, employment or other benefit"" in exchange for a vote. It would impose a maximum 
penalty of $20,000 for a first offence and $30,000 for any subsequent offence.
Trading cash for votes is already illegal during a general election.
Vote-buying allegations surfaced in late November, when the Journal de Montréal published text messages 
between two unnamed people that suggested some voters had been paid $100 each to support Rodriguez.
While the Journal didn't name the individuals, Cogeco political analyst Jonathan Trudeau said the exchange was 
between Liberal MNA Sona Lakhoyan Olivier and Coalition Avenir Québec MNA Alice Abou-Khalil, who had been 
rumoured to have been trying to join the Liberals ahead of the 2026 election.

leadership.

Wednesday.
Drama has been brewing within the official opposition party since early last week, when Marwah Rizqy, 
parliamentary leader and MNA for St-Laurent, fired chief of staff Geneviève Hinse( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/genevieve-hinse-pablo-rodriguez-quebec-liberals ).
In the time since, Rizqy was ousted from her role as parliamentary leader by party leader Pablo Rodriguez; Hinse 
fired back at Rizqy( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rizqy-hinse-lawyer-letter ) 
with a legal letter, then sued her; and it was revealed that the firing may have been related to the alleged misuse of 
National Assembly funds for partisan activities.
The turmoil in the party comes ahead of the 2026 provincial election, when Rodriguez plans to run for a seat in the 
National Assembly.
Here's a timeline of events thus far:
June 14: Quebec Liberals elect Rodriguez( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-liberals-choose-pablo-
rodriguez-as-new-leader ), former federal Liberal MP from Montreal,( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-
liberals-choose-pablo-rodriguez-as-new-leader ) as the new leader of the party. He won with 52.3 per cent of the 
vote, narrowly overtaking contender Charles Milliard, who received 47.7 per cent of the vote.
June 19: Rodriguez selects Rizqy( https://montrealgazette.com/news/pablo-rodriguez-picks-marwah-rizqy-to-lead-
liberals-in-legislature ) - known for her ability to hold the Coalition Avenir Québec government's feet to the fire - to 
lead the party in the National Assembly since he's not an MNA.
Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury, highlighted left, and Liberal MNA Marwah Rizqy among a group of politicians posing 
for photos during an inauguration event for the the Deux-Montagnes branch of the REM in Deux-Montagnes on 
Nov. 14, 2025.

Nov. 14: Federal, provincial and local politicians attend a ceremony for the opening of the REM's long-awaited 
Deux-Montagnes branch. A discussion between Rizqy and Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury may have sparked the 
drama that unfolded days later, according to La Presse. El-Khoury denied having a discussion with Rizqy about 
Rodriguez's leadership race and insisted he had no connection to the campaign, but La Presse later discovered he 
had raised funds for Rodriguez.
Nov. 17: Rizqy fires her chief of staff in a short email to members of the Liberal caucus, taking the party by surprise.
""We would like to inform you that Mme. Geneviève Hinse ... is no longer employed as chief of staff of the leader of 
the official opposition as of now,"" the email read.
La Presse reported the dismissal was related to the alleged use of the party's National Assembly budget to pay for 
partisan activities like Rodriguez's recent tour of the regions, which isn't permitted.
Nov. 18: Rodriguez ousts Rizqy as parliamentary leader over the firing of Hinse, claiming he wasn't consulted or 
given an explanation. Hinse was Rodriguez's chief of staff when he was a federal politician and decided to follow 
him into Quebec politics.
Rodriguez's decision to oust Rizqy, ""while difficult, was necessary to ensure the cohesion and the good functioning 
of the Liberal caucus at the National Assembly,"" the party said in a statement.
Rizqy was replaced as parliamentary leader by Pontiac MNA André Fortin. She remains a Liberal but is suspended 
from the caucus until further notice.
Geneviève Hinse in 2019.
Nov. 19: Hinse fires back with a legal letter giving Rizqy 24 hours to admit the ""absence of justified motive"" for the 
firing, warning that she may sue her if she refuses.
In the letter, Rizqy is accused of violating the customs of the party by firing Hinse because such decisions are 
supposed to be made by the party leader.
Before the letter came out, Hinse defended herself in a statement: ""I am obviously hurt by this situation, especially 
since I know nothing justifies my firing.""
The same day, the Journal de Montréal reported( https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2025/11/19/il-faut-encore-
payer-pour-que-le-monde-vote-pablo-des-textos-troublants-derriere-la-crise-au-plq ) Élections Québec was looking 
into text messages insinuating Liberal Party members were paid to vote Rodriguez in as leader.
One exchange reads:
""So, everyone's going to get paid (this) week?""
""Yes. And don't forget, we're only returning the membership cards on May 8 in case something goes wrong. All 
that's left is the voting process and they get a brownie for voting.""
A $100 bill is sometimes referred to as a ""brownie"" in slang.
Cogeco political analyst Jonathan Trudeau claimed the exchanges were between Alice Abou-Khalil, CAQ MNA for 
Fabre, and Sona Lakhoyan Olivier, Liberal MNA for Chomedey, both of whom denied the accusations.
Rodriguez called in an external auditor to investigate the Journal report, saying he had no knowledge of the 
allegations.
""We have nothing to hide,"" he said at the time. ""I have nothing to hide. Nobody has anything to hide.""

According to the Directeur général des élections du Québec, there are no rules against someone being 
compensated for voting for a candidate in a leadership race (though, it's not allowed in general elections or 
byelections).
Premier François Legault and Rodriguez have both since said they'd be in favour of having the law changed if it's 
considered legal to buy votes.
Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez speaks to media while surrounded by the Liberal caucus in Montreal on 
Friday, Nov. 21, 2025. The caucus was held in the aftermath of vote-buying allegations and other turmoil in the 
party that continued throughout the week.
Nov. 21: Rodriguez says the party might take the Journal de Montréal to court unless it shares more information 
about the alleged vote-buying scheme, requesting the names and phone numbers from the text exchange.
""You cannot just put things like that in a paper and accuse people,"" he said.
Also on this day, Cogeco journalist Louis Lacroix read a letter on air from Rizqy's lawyers to those of Hinse, 
defending the firing. The lawyers declined to share a copy of the letter with The Gazette but confirmed one had 
been sent. According to Lacroix, the letter said the decision was made after reviews of many ""concerning situations"" 
related to the performance of Hinse's duties, conduct and obligations as chief of staff.
""Your client's dismissal was imposed due to significant ethical breaches, particularly with regard to compliance with 
the standards of the National Assembly of Quebec, the internal procedures and expectations related to her 
position,"" the letter said. ""In addition, there were repeated acts of insubordination, including non-compliance with 
clear instructions issued by our client. Notably, your client refused to follow our client's directive to consult with the 
ethics commissioner.""
Lacroix said the letter noted Rizqy couldn't say Hinse had been fired without motive ""because that would be a false 
and erroneous declaration.""
Later that day, Hinse claimed $500,000 in moral and punitive damages against Rizqy. She claims it was Rizqy who 
acted in bad faith and ""completely resisted"" attempts to go to the National Assembly's ethics commissioner to clear 
up operational issues, including what spending should be covered by public funds and what should be considered 
partisan activities paid for by the party.
The claim says Rizqy resisted because she didn't have confidence in the ethics commissioner to ""open such a 
dialogue,"" based on her personal experience with the commissioner and that of her husband, Jacques-Cartier MNA 
Greg Kelley.
""A conflict of personalities developed between the two, fed by Mme. Rizqy's mood swings,"" the claim states.
When Hinse presented a document outlining an operational plan for such spending, Rizqy refused to touch it. It was 
shortly after that incident that she received the letter from Rizqy informing her she was fired.
The claim also notes that if Rizqy apologizes in writing and admits the ""existence of a grave error"" on her part in 
firing Hinse, she would drop the case.
Nov. 23: Rizqy breaks her silence, insisting that she acted within her right and pointing out that she's not allowed to 
discuss human resources matters publicly.
That night, Rodriguez appears on Radio-Canada talk show Tout le monde en parle, saying Rizqy had spoken to 
him about some kind of political ""fling flang"" (or funny business) linked to Ottawa.

Nov. 26: In the wake of the La Presse report tying the tension within the party back to the REM inauguration, 
Rodriguez acknowledges that El-Khoury raised funds for his leadership race. He noted El-Khoury's activities were 
legal because he had a campaign certificate permitting him to raise funds.
""He raised money like lots of people,"" Rodriguez said.
El-Khoury did not respond to The Gazette's request for comment Wednesday and refused to answer questions from 
reporters outside the federal Liberal caucus in Ottawa, but told La Presse his comments may have been 
""ambiguous"" last week. He said he assumed he was being asked if he helped acquire membership cards for 
Rodriguez, which he said he didn't. That's why he said he was never involved in the campaign.

year and the fact that she had been an inspiration to his daughter, who is thinking of entering politics.
Later in the day, Quebec's Unité permanente anticorruption (UPAC) confirms it is verifying ""allegations of 
reprehensible acts targeting the Liberal Party of Quebec"" but has not yet launched a formal investigation. 
""Following the analysis of this information, we will be able to take a decision to know if we need to go further with 
the investigation or not.""
Rodriguez says he will fully co-operate with UPAC. ""If someone, somewhere, committed an illegal act or contrary to 
our ethics, the truth must come out and we will fully co-operate. If shortcomings are revealed, I will act. There is no 
place for this in the Liberal Party of Quebec. Tolerance zero. Period,"" he writes in a social media post.

QUEBEC - The day after the province's anticorruption unit confirmed it was meeting witnesses in connection with 
allegations against the Quebec Liberal Party, leader Pablo Rodriguez said his opponents were playing a ""political 
game.""
Speaking to reporters Thursday morning, Québec solidaire MNA Alejandra Zaga Mendez was playing show and 
tell, holding up a copy of PLQ Inc., a 2019 book that investigated allegations into corruption in the Quebec Liberal 
Party under former premier Jean Charest.
""When we see UPAC and the Liberal Party of Quebec in the same newspaper headline, it reminds us of just one 
thing,"" she said. ""Every day, we wake up and we learn of a new scandal in the Liberal Party of Quebec.""
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon accused the Liberal party of a ""culture of corruption,"" which he 
said stemmed from a loyalty to the ""Canadian regime.""
Rodriguez rejected St-Pierre Plamondon's assertion, defining his party as the oldest in Quebec, ""the party of the 
economy"" and ""the party of a just society.""
Québec solidaire's reference to alleged corruption under Charest ""is just their political game,"" Rodriguez said, 
""because they don't have anything else to say.""
First reported in the Journal de Montréal, the Unité permanente anticorruption (UPAC) confirmed Wednesday that it 
was looking into fundraising allegations involving the Quebec Liberal Party, but stressed that it hadn't started a 
formal investigation.
The Journal reported Thursday that UPAC had met with Marwah Rizqy, who Pablo Rodriguez removed from her 
post as parliamentary leader after she fired Geneviève Hinse, her chief of staff. Rodriguez maintained Thursday 
that he still didn't know why Rizqy had removed Hinse.
If UPAC proceeds with an investigation, ""we're going to collaborate,"" he promised. ""We have nothing to hide.""
A Pallas Data poll published by L'actualité on Wednesday showed only 13 per cent of Quebecers have a favourable 
impression of Rodriguez - placing him behind Plamondon, Québec solidaire's Ruba Ghazal and Quebec 
Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime - and tying him with Premier François Legault.

QUÉBEC - The Quebec Liberals have lost two members of their caucus within a week and are facing multiple 
investigations as a crisis within the party shows no sign of abating.
The Liberals have been dogged by controversy for nearly three weeks, with one recent poll showing the party and 
its leader, former federal cabinet minister Pablo Rodriguez, have taken a substantial hit in public opinion. 
""Everything that's coming out now, it's preventing us from doing our best work,"" Monsef Derraji, a Liberal member of 
the legislature, told reporters in Quebec City on Friday. ""I'm tired of hearing all these stories every day.""
His comments came after Rodriguez announced Thursday evening that he had expelled a Montreal-area member 
of the legislature, Sona Lakhoyan Olivier, from his caucus because she is under investigation by Quebec's ethics 
commissioner. 
The office of the ethics commissioner announced it will investigate whether Lakhoyan Olivier used resources from 
her constituency office for partisan purposes during this year's Liberal leadership race, which Rodriguez won in 
June. 
""Under the circumstances, I have decided to exclude her from the Quebec Liberal Party caucus for the duration of 
this investigation,"" Rodriguez said on X. 
Lakhoyan Olivier wrote on social media Thursday that she has always followed the rules and will co-operate fully 
with the investigation.
At a press conference on Friday, Marc Tanguay, the party's chief whip, said it's customary for members of the 
legislature to be removed from their caucus while they're subject to ethics investigations. 
Another Liberal, Désirée McGraw, told reporters the Liberal caucus remains ""100 per cent"" behind Rodriguez. 
Still, that caucus now numbers just 18 people after Rodriguez expelled his former parliamentary leader, Marwah 
Rizqy, earlier this week, saying she lacked loyalty to him and to the party. 
Rizqy kicked off the crisis in the Liberal ranks when she fired her chief of staff last month. Rodriguez says she did 
not consult with him about the decision and has not explained her reasons.

The Liberals are also facing allegations of possible vote-buying during the leadership race. Last month, Le Journal 
de Montréal published text messages suggesting some party members who voted for Rodriguez could have 
received cash rewards.
Montreal radio station 98.5 FM named Lakhoyan Olivier as one of the two people behind those text messages, but 
she has denied that claim and has sent a legal letter to station owner Cogeco.
The Canadian Press has not verified whether the text messages were authentic. It's also unclear whether the firing 
of Rizqy's chief of staff and the vote-buying allegations are connected. 
Rodriguez has asked a retired judge to investigate the allegations, and says anyone involved in such activity will be 
kicked out of the party. Quebec's anticorruption police have also said they are looking into the controversy. 
The crisis for the Liberals comes as the party tries to regain the support of Quebec voters, particularly 
francophones outside Montreal, ahead of next year's election. With the governing Coalition Avenir Québec polling 
badly, the Liberals are positioning themselves as the alternative to the Parti Québécois, which is promising a 
referendum on independence by 2030. 
But a recent Léger/Québecor poll showed the Liberals losing ground as the controversy drags on. The survey put 
the Liberals at 21 per cent, compared to 39 per cent for the PQ.
On Friday, the Quebec government tabled new legislation to ban vote-buying in leadership and nomination races. 
To the surprise of many lawmakers, Elections Quebec recently revealed that the province’s Elections Act does not 
prohibit people from making donations in exchange for votes in those campaigns. 
The bill, which has the support of the opposition parties, includes fines of up to $10,000 for a first offence and up to 
$30,000 for repeat offences within 10 years.

The Ford government has fired the entire board of directors at Ontario's real estate regulator to fix what the 
premier on Monday called ""a total mess.""
The Real Estate Council of Ontario (RECO) confirmed to the Star all eight members of its board ""cease to hold 
office upon the appointment of the Administrator."" 
Jean Lépine, who started this week as the administrator, was appointed by the province, which formally assumed 
control of the organization on Monday in the wake of the iPro scandal.
Stephen Crawford, minister of public and business service delivery and procurement, which oversees the 
regulator, gave Lépine ""exclusive right to exercise all the powers and perform all the duties of the board, officers, 
and members of RECO,"" he wrote in a Nov. 28 letter to the regulator's board chair Katie Steinfeld and CEO Brenda 
Buchanan.
In a brief written statement on Monday, Lépine said he will spend the next several weeks ""engaging across the 
sector to listen, learn, and gather insights"" that will help him restore public confidence in RECO. 
A formal minister's order dated Sunday and made public Monday sets out the board's dismissal and the terms of 
Lépine's appointment, for which he will earn $2,000 per day.
The order does not explicitly say who else within RECO may soon be out of a job, but several industry insiders told 
the Star the administrator is expected to ""clean house."" 
Lépine's appointment followed widespread concerns about the regulator's ability to protect consumers from theft 
and fraud in the wake of the iPro Realty scandal, which saw the co-founders of one of Ontario's largest 
brokerages strike a deal with RECO to evade charges and fines after they ""illegally disbursed"" more than $10 
million from the company's trust accounts, which held consumer deposits.
RECO failed to immediately alert the public to what it called an unprecedented financial breach. Instead, it allowed 
iPro co-founders Rui Alves, a former RECO board member, and Fedele Colucci to continue operating their 
business for three months, transacting more than $700 million in residential real estate sales, a Star investigation 
reported.
