Stephen Anderson, who co-founded Global Health Imports with Boissonnault at the start of the pandemic in 2020, 
and Kirsten Poon, a lobbyist with business ties to the minister, will be appearing before the House of Commons 
ethics committee for an hour. At issue is whether Boissonnault remained an active participant in the medical supply 
business he co-owned after he was appointed to cabinet, which would have violated ethics rules.
Poon is scheduled to appear at the committee virtually, but Anderson is expected to testify in person.

""We've been looking to find out information that, frankly... Boissonnault has refused to provide, and he has 
demonstrated himself to be not forthcoming on matters that are certainly in the public interest,"" said Conservative 
ethics critic Michael Barrett.
The NDP's Matthew Green said in a statement there is ""clearly more for the committee to study in the minister's

Weeks after Delta's 2018 municipal election, newly elected Mayor George Harvie raised eyebrows when he hired 
his running mate, Paramjit Singh Grewal, to be his executive assistant with a $130,000 salary.
At that time, some political rivals decried the hiring( https://www.surreynowleader.com/news/delta-mayor-hires-
former-running-mate-as-executive-assistant-2942761 ) as patronage.
Four years later, within weeks of Harvie's re-election to a second term, Grewal was promoted to the newly created 
role of general manager of economic development and stakeholder relations. His $234,000 salary made him one of 
the city's highest paid employees, although he managed no staff members and apparently produced no reports for 
city council.
Grewal was fired in March, and sued the city for wrongful dismissal in April.
Now, Grewal appears to have found himself in the middle of a political battle between Delta politicians. He says he 
doesn't know why.
In May, after a group of Delta councillors made the stunning move( https://vancouversun.com/news/local-news/loss-
of-confidence-in-delta-mayor-leads-to-governance-change-councillors-say ) to strip Harvie of his role with Metro 
Vancouver and limit the powers of his office, both sides of that battle mentioned Grewal's lawsuit in their public 
comments.
The councillors' statement mentioned ""serious personnel issues"" before the courts, while Harvie said he was ""very 
disappointed"" council was involved in Grewal's suit. But neither side publicly explained how Grewal's dismissal and 
lawsuit related to the councillors' move against Harvie( https://vancouversun.com/news/local-news/delta-
councillors-break-silence-over-stripping-mayor-of-metro-vancouver-role ).
Grewal, when asked that question, said this week: ""I'm also trying to find that out.""
Grewal declined to discuss the work he did at city hall or the lawsuit.
""Right now, my only focus is on ensuring that I have my day in court,"" Grewal said. ""All the juicy bits are going to 
come out in court. And I can't wait for my day.""

Grewal's notice of claim describes several comments Kruger is alleged to have made to an unnamed person

In that conversation, Kruger allegedly said Grewal was engaged in ""a huge conflict of interest,"" tried to pressure 
city officials to rezone property and ""change recommendations to personally benefit"" himself, and tried to ""interfere 
in the planning process,"" Grewal's lawsuit says.
The suit alleges Kruger told Witness No. 1 that Grewal had ""serious, serious personality related problems"" and was

into tears, on top of other performance related problems.""
Kruger's newly filed response to the lawsuit alleges that the unnamed Witness No. 1 was ""engaged"" by Grewal, for 
the ""improper purpose of eliciting statements for this action.""
The witness is also not named in Kruger's response, but is described as a Delta resident and businessperson who 
was ""very engaged and involved in Delta civic matters."" The witness contacted Kruger a few days after Grewal's 
termination, making ""persistent inquiries"" about the matter. Kruger's response says he met the man over coffee, 
and didn't divulge any confidential information from the in-camera meeting, but shared his ""honestly held beliefs and 
genuine concerns"" about Grewal's conduct and performance, ""including what he had witnessed.""
""At the conclusion of the coffee meeting, Witness No. 1 appeared to have stopped a recording on his phone,"" 
Kruger's response says.
Grewal has worked in various capacities in Delta-area politics for more than 20 years. Before his unsuccessful 
council run in 2018 with Harvie's slate, Grewal had worked in the constituency offices of B.C. NDP MLAs.

newly created role"" and no staff members reported to him. Since Grewal's termination in March ""the city has not

dozens of reports produced by other GMs of other departments, but none from Grewal or his office.

comment.
Former Delta councillor Sylvia Bishop said it's ""very odd"" for a GM to manage no staff and produce no reports.
""All other GMs write reports and let us know what's going on, and all of that is available to the public. But not this 
one,"" said Bishop, who spent seven years on council before running for mayor against Harvie in 2018. ""This is 
absolutely outrageous that this person was hired for that kind of a job at that kind of a salary.""

Dozens of protesters staged a demonstration in front of a Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE) office north 
of Toronto on Tuesday to demand the resignation of Fred Hahn over an antisemitic video the national vice president 
shared on social media.
The protesters chanted ""Fire Fred"" and ""Fred Must Go"" outside the union's Ontario office in Thornhill. Some waved 
Israeli and Canadian flags and carried placards, one of which read, ""Public employees deserve much more than a 
Jew hater.""
Hahn, who has also led CUPE Ontario, a political branch of CUPE National, since 2010, shared a video on social 
media earlier this month that has been widely condemned by Jewish communities and government officials as 
antisemitic.
""It's vile and shocking,"" said Amir Epstein, an executive director of Tafsik, ahead of the rally. The grassroots 
organization dedicated to combating an alarming rise of antisemitism globally, organized the protest. ""It's unheard 
of that someone in such a powerful position in Canada can openly disrespect the Jewish community. He needs to 
resign.""
People rally in support of Israel and protest against CUPE Ontario President Fred Hahn in Richmond Hill, Tuesday

The rally, predominantly attended by members of the Jewish community, also drew support from various allied 
groups.
One of the speakers was Salman Sima, a former political prisoner from Iran. He said that there should be no room 
for hatred and antisemitism in Canada. ""Unlike the useless, cowardly, corrupt, and incompetent politicians at all 
levels of government, when we say there is no room for hatred in Canada, when we say there is no room for hatred 
in Ontario, we walk the talk,"" Sima said. ""I'm not afraid to say that Fred must go.""
Another protester, Charles Cooke, a government relations representative for the Canadian Antisemitism Education 
Foundation, learned about Tuesday's rally through social media. He attended to condemn Hahn's remarks. ""He 
leads CUPE in Ontario, and it's completely unacceptable that we have a union leader in Canada, in Ontario, 
spewing brazen hate toward any community. It wouldn't be tolerated with any other group,"" Cooke said. ""That's why 
we are here.""

A B.C. Supreme Court judge has turned down an attempt by an Iranian national to stop his extradition to the U.S. to 
face fraud and money laundering charges there.
Justice Janet Winteringham did agree with the lawyer for Seyed Abood Sari, who said Sari's consular rights were 
infringed upon during his arrest when he landed at YVR in January 2019 to celebrate his birthday with his two sons 
attending university in B.C.
The Canada Border Services Agency detained Sari when he arrived in Canada because it had learned he was a 
principal employee of Mahan Air, an Iranian airline sanctioned under Canada's anti-terrorism regulations, she 
wrote.
That would make him inadmissible to Canada under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, although Sari 
denied then and since that he worked for the airline, the decision said.
CBSA said it learned hours after his arrival that there was a U.S. warrant for charges of fraud and money 
laundering, it said.
At Sari's detention review hearing, the federal immigration minister extended his detention to further investigate 
whether the basis of those charges would also make him inadmissible to Canada, the reasons said.
Winteringham also said in her ruling there were concerns about how his detention hearings were conducted, which 
led to Sari spending six months in pretrial custody before being let out on bail under strict conditions, including 
electronic monitoring.
But she said the violations in both instances weren't serious enough to warrant a stay of extradition proceedings 
against Sari.
Lawyers for Sari argued before the court that his detention should be considered an abuse of process because he 
was denied his right to access the Iranian embassy as required under the Vienna Convention on Consular 
Relations, the decision said.
Winteringham agreed there was an infringement of his consular rights under the convention but, she wrote, ""I have 
concluded, however, that this failure does not warrant a stay of the extradition proceedings.""

what the police force said was ""one of the most complex investigations that the service has experienced in its 
history.""
""The subjects face charges of fraud over $5,000, trafficking in identifying information, possession of identifying 
information and identity theft. For example, the investigation revealed that one of the subjects had in his possession 
a list of data targeting 1.6 million Quebecers,"" Laval police said in a statement. ""This exhaustive investigation, 
carried out by Laval police officers since December 2018, aimed to investigate the fraudulent appropriation by a 
group of individuals, via the Accès D de Desjardins website, of sums held in the accounts of several members of 
the financial institution.""
The fraudsters were able to use Desjardins's website to obtain temporary passwords with the personal information 
that was stolen. They then made transactions directly from bank accounts.
""These frauds, mainly affecting Desjardins business accounts, were committed mainly during the period from 
September 2018 to January 2019. The amount of fraud against Desjardins and its members amounts to more than 
$8.9 million,"" Laval police wrote.
During the investigation, police carried out seven search warrants, during 2019, in Laval, Montreal and St-Augustin-
de-Desmaures. The searches turned up what the Laval police described as ""a significant quantity of data, both in 
the form of tangible documents and computer files.""

of St-Augustin-de-Desmaures, was released on a promise to appear in court at a later date.

and its members out of more than $5,000 between Sept. 4, 2018 and Jan. 10, 2019.

OTTAWA - Could a member of the intelligence oversight committee claim parliamentary privilege to reveal 
classified intelligence in the House of Commons and be immune from prosecution? That's a question that could be 
headed to the Supreme Court of Canada.
The issue has surely never been more relevant than now, given the release last week of the committee's bombshell 
foreign interference report( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/foreign-interference-committee-report-released ) 
alleging that some parliamentarians ""wittingly"" conspired with other governments.
In a late April ruling that largely went unnoticed( https://nationalpost.com/opinion/colby-cosh-parliamentarians-
absolute-right-to-free-speech-not-absolute-court-says ), the Ontario Court of Appeal ruled that legislators on the 
National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians (NSICOP) cannot claim parliamentary immunity if 
they ""improperly"" reveal state secrets obtained through their work.
The ruling has new and significant implications for the ongoing debate about revealing classified information 
following NSICOP's report released on June 3. The case has pit national security against the vital principle of 
parliamentary privilege in a Westminster-style democracy, which gives legislators immunity for actions undertaken 
as part of their duties.
But the issue may be far from closed, as Lakehead University constitutional law professor Ryan Alford said he plans 
on asking the country's top court to hear his appeal of the decision.
In April, a panel of three appeal court judges ruled that Parliament was within its rights( 
https://www.canlii.org/en/on/onca/doc/2024/2024onca306/2024onca306.html ) when it included a clause in the 
NSICOP Act that excludes legislators on the committee from parliamentary immunity if they divulge sensitive 
information without the proper authority.
That could include, for example, revealing in the House of Commons which parliamentarians are suspected by 
intelligence agencies of having wittingly aided a foreign government contrary to the interests of Canada.
The appeal court conceded that the exclusion contained in the NSICOP Act ""does limit the right to free speech and 
debate within Parliament,"" but that it wasn't unconstitutional.

A bipartisan group of U.S. senators sent a letter Wednesday to the leader of the World Anti-Doping Agency asking 
for answers about the case in which 23 Chinese swimmers were cleared to compete at the Tokyo Olympics despite 
positive tests for a banned drug.
That letter came a day after a bipartisan group from the House sent a similar request to IOC President Thomas 
Bach and a letter to Attorney General Merrick Garland and FBI Director Christopher Wray asking for a briefing on 
federal investigators' knowledge of the case.
“It is not just this one incident that causes concern for many athletes, anti-doping agencies, and fans across the 
world, but it is the fact that WADA has long shown questionable ethical behavior,” said the letter sent from Sens. 
Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., and Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.
Last month, German broadcaster ARD and the New York Times reported that Chinese authorities determined the 
swimmers who had tested positive for a banned heart medication would not be punished because they had 
accidentally ingested the banned heart medication found in a hotel kitchen.
The story triggered a harsh backlash from WADA critics who said the agency did not follow its own rules when it 
decided to accept China's explanation for the positives instead of further pursuing the case. WADA has argued it 
handled the case appropriately and that, given the circumstances, it would have had virtually no chance of winning 
the case on appeal. 
Three of the swimmers who were cleared won gold medals less than a year later in Tokyo.
“This scandal raises serious legal, ethical, and competitive concerns and may constitute a broader state-sponsored 
strategy by the People’s Republic of China (PRC) to unfairly compete at the Olympic Games,"" Reps. John 
Moolenaar, R-Mich., and Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., wrote to Wray and Garland.
Moolenaar is chair and Krishnamoorthi is ranking member on the House Select Committee on the Chinese 
Communist Party.

Doug Ford is having one funny summer.
Funny as in politically peculiar - without having much fun or hearing many laughs from the home crowd.
First, he appealed to people not to ""go pooping"" on Wasaga Beach. It made late-night TV in the U.S. as a laugh 
line, but locals squirmed.
Then Ford joked that a new animal hospital in King City could reduce lineups for humans needing health care. His 
ribbon-cutting audience was polite, but the line fell flat in Ontario's overcrowded hospitals.
After the negative headlines, the premier was poised to party last Friday night, giving out free food and drinks to a 
""Ford Fest"" crowd in Milton. But just before party time, it was quitting time for popular education minister Todd 
Smith, who left a big hole in cabinet by bailing out on short notice.
If the summer of 2024 feels unfunny, the summer of 2025 might be that much more miserable. For all the fuss 
about Ford's latest wisecracks in the news media, there is bigger (and badder) news behind the scenes.
The premier must be - should be - paying attention.
As the Star's Robert Benzie has revealed, a quiet RCMP investigation is fast gaining momentum, gathering critical 
statements about alleged wrongdoing in the $8.28-billion Greenbelt imbroglio of two summers ago. By next 
summer, rather than parsing the premier's laugh lines and press lines, the media may be writing more about the 
police line of inquiry at Queen's Park.
Interviews with members of the RCMP ""O"" Division's Sensitive and International Investigations unit, the elite 
Ottawa-based branch that probes political crimes and corruption, are taking place in the Greater Toronto Area. 
While the force remains tight-lipped, sources say that current and former staff in Ford's Progressive Conservative 
government are systematically being questioned about the controversial land swap.
The probe comes in the wake of a devastating report by the provincial auditor general last summer, which placed 
an $8.28-billion value on the windfall from Ford's Tories opening up previously protected lands to development. 
Ford has gone back and forth on the Greenbelt - first declaring open season on its protected lands in early 2018, 
then reversing himself pre-election, then doing a U-turn upon re-election in 2022, and finally backing off again last 
year after the auditor's bombshell report landed.
Page 2 of 3
Premier's Greenbelt woes no laughing matter
For all his zigzags, Ford's apologia eased the public pressure - his polling numbers bounced back to record highs. 
But the police pressure isn't going away.
Indeed, the RCMP probe appears to be a major consideration behind Ford's remarkable game plan to call an 
election as early as next spring. That would be more than a year ahead of the fixed election date mandated by law 
for June 2026.
What political pretext could Ford's Tories conjure up to seek a fresh mandate? How could a government that won 
re-election with a massive majority a mere two years ago justify going back into pre-election mode so early in the 
legislative cycle?
Ford's priority, bizarrely, is the boutique issue of beer in corner stores, given his determination to ""keep the 
promise"" he made in 2018 after allowing it to languish for so many years. That decision came at considerable cost - 
hundreds of millions of dollars to pacify the Beer Store (and the big brewers that own it) in order to move up the 
2026 end date for a previous contract governing beer sales.
There are other distortions and contortions tied to Ford's fear of an RCMP probe. Remember that the premier 
came to power by promising to clean up what he claimed was corruption by the previous Liberal government of 
Kathleen Wynne giving preferential treatment to insiders and political friends, though he never produced any 
evidence; now the tables may be turned on the Tories.
The allegations of racketeering and distractions of electioneering are stressing out the Tories, and the loss of 
influential cabinet ministers doesn't help: Smith's departure will weaken the government at the very time it is trying 
to put its best face(s) forward.
As Ontario's long-serving energy minister, he kept the Tories out of trouble by disarming the opposition and 
stakeholders alike. But Smith was reluctant to soldier on when shuffled to the education portfolio this summer.
The ministerial heavyweights who left before him - Monte McNaughton, Rod Phillips and Christine Elliott - have also 
left big gaps at the cabinet table and on the front benches. In their places, Ford has opted for quantity over quality, 
appointing the most bloated cabinet in the province's history with a record 37 members.
Ford may yet prove the doubters wrong, romping to yet another election victory next spring. Perhaps he'll be sitting 
pretty by next summer, should the RCMP come calling for top Tories in and out of government.
But it doesn't sound like much fun.

OTTAWA - Government organizations frequently disregarded federal contracting and procurement rules when 
awarding contracts to consulting firm McKinsey & Company, the auditor general concluded in a report released 
Tuesday.
At the request of the House of Commons, auditor general Karen Hogan probed 97 contracts awarded to McKinsey 
between 2011 and 2023, with a total value of $209 million.
Federal contracts with McKinsey came under scrutiny last year after media reports highlighted the rapid growth of 
the company's work under Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's Liberal government.
The audit found nine out of 10 departments and agencies, as well as eight out of 10 Crown corporations, failed to 
follow all aspects of their own procurement policies and guidelines on at least one contract.
Organizations also didn't justify the fact there was no competitive process for 18 out of 19 contracts that went 
directly to the consulting firm, the auditor found.
And the government may not be getting value for its money, the auditor flagged, noting that in a sample of 33 
contracts, the cost was not estimated in advance for 30 of them.
Hogan offered one recommendation on strengthening conflict-of-interest rules, which the federal government 
accepted.
She said the government doesn't need to layer new rules onto existing ones, but rather, it needs to ensure its 
existing policies are followed.
The federal funds that went to McKinsey amount to only 0.27 per cent of the total amount spent on consultants for 
similar services, the auditor said. 
Contracts with McKinsey came under particular scrutiny because of the firm's former global managing director's link 
to the Liberal government, which raised questions about what influence McKinsey had on public policy.
However, Hogan said the pattern of non-compliance existed before the Trudeau government was elected.

Page 2 of 3

""We saw non-compliance, either with procurement rules or difficulty demonstrating value for money, throughout the 
whole 12-year period of time,"" Hogan said, describing a pervasive pattern across government organizations.
""That's why I have the belief that it isn't limited to McKinsey, it is likely a bigger issue of making sure that the rules 
are not forgotten, and people are paying attention to them.""
Nevertheless, Conservatives pinned the auditor general's findings squarely on the Liberal government. 
""It's not a surprise that Trudeau gave McKinsey hundreds of millions of dollars. At the time, McKinsey was led by 
Dominic Barton, a close friend and adviser of Justin Trudeau and Chrystia Freeland,"" a statement from the 
Conservatives said.
Meanwhile, NDP Treasury Board critic Blake Desjarlais said the report revealed that consecutive Conservative and 
Liberal governments ""have been favouring McKinsey over professional public service workers."" 
""New Democrats are calling on the Liberals to strengthen the procurement process and make it more transparent 
for Canadians, and not just to benefit their ultrarich Bay Street friends.""
Procurement Minister Jean-Yves Duclos outlined some of the steps the government has taken to strengthen its 
contracting processes, including increasing scrutiny on contracts awarded as part of a non-competitive process. 
""I will also note that we have created a new position of chief contract quality assurance and records compliance 
office. That action would ensure that critical elements of decision-making throughout the procurement process are 
properly documented, that guidelines and tools are put in place and that quality is being actively monitored,"" Duclos 
said at a news conference Tuesday,
The Treasury Board released a report last year that reviewed contracts awarded to McKinsey. 
The departmental audits found no evidence of political interference and no evidence that the integrity of the 
procurement process was not maintained, the Treasury Board's final report said last year.
But they did find some administrative requirements and procedures were not consistently followed.
In a separate audit released Tuesday, Hogan found an arm's-length foundation that's supposed to award funds to 
develop new climate-change technology handed out money for ineligible projects. 
Of the 58 Sustainable Development Technology Canada projects the auditor looked at, 10 were ineligible but got 
funding anyway. Those 10 projects received a total of $59 million.
Innovation Minister François-Philippe Champagne said it was Parliament's decision to deliver the funds through an 
arm's length agency 20 years ago.
After several investigations, including the auditor's, the government has proposed a new model, he said.
""We're going to move the activity to the National Research Council, and this has (a) number of benefits,"" the 
minister said Tuesday. 
""One of which is that they're going to be subject to (the) Treasury Board's rules in terms of how you manage public 
funds.""
This report by The Canadian Press was first published June 4, 2024.

QUEBEC - In the wake of the legal challenge to Bill 21, Quebec's state secularism law, Quebec Justice Minister 
Simon Jolin-Barrette is asking Supreme Court Judge Mahmud Jamal to recuse himself, fearing that he ""does not 
have the impartiality required to hear this case.""
The information, first reported by Le Devoir( https://www.ledevoir.com/societe/justice/815946/tour-quebec-exiger-
recusation-juge-jamal ), was confirmed by The Canadian Press.
In a letter sent to the Supreme Court on Wednesday, Jolin-Barrette says Jamal was the president of the Canadian 
Civil Liberties Association when it filed an appeal before the Superior Court to challenge the Act Respecting the 
Laicity of the State in June 2019.
The act prohibits state employees in positions of authority - including teachers - from wearing visible religious 
symbols such as the Muslim veil, Jewish kippah, Sikh turban and Christian crosses while working.
""As president of the association, Judge Jamal was necessarily involved in some way in the preparation of this 194-
paragraph procedure, whether in its drafting, its revision or simply to approve its content,"" reads the letter, a copy of 
which was obtained by The Canadian Press.
The letter also says ""the fact that Judge Jamal must decide questions of constitutional law raised by the association 
at the time when he presided over it means that today he would be the judge in a case in which he was a party.""
The Canadian Press also obtained letters from the Mouvement laïque québécois (MLQ) and the group Pour les 
droits des femmes du Québec (PDF Québec), which also call for the Jamal's recusal for similar reasons.
But in a letter dated June 25, the Supreme Court said Jamal did not intend to step down. ""(He) considers that there 
is no real or reasonably perceptible conflict of interest that would prompt him to recuse himself,"" reads the letter, a 
copy of which The Canadian Press also obtained.
Jamal was appointed a judge to the Supreme Court of Canada on July 1, 2021. He previously served as a judge at 
the Ontario Court of Appeal from 2019 to 2021, according to the Supreme Court website. Before being appointed a 
judge, Jamal was an attorney with the firm of Osler, Hoskin &; Harcourt.
Page 2 of 3
Quebec asks for Supreme Court judge to recuse himself on Bill 21
Several groups, including the CCLA, have asked the Supreme Court to review the judgment of the Quebec Court of 
Appeal regarding Bill 21. The country's highest court has not yet indicated whether it is going to take up the matter 
or not.
The federal government has already said it would participate in a possible legal challenge to Bill 21 before the 
Supreme Court, while the Quebec government has always promised to defend the secularism of the state ""to the 
end.""
In February, the Court of Appeal validated almost all of Bill 21( https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/bill-21-
upheld-deemed-constitutional-by-quebec-court-of-appeal ), affirming that it does not violate the linguistic rights of 
English-speaking school boards.
The Court of Appeal also affirmed that Quebec had the right to use the Charter's notwithstanding clause in a 
preventive manner as it did in the case of Bill 21.
This was a significant setback for opponents of this legislation.

Chestermere residents will head to the polls on Monday, tasked with choosing their next mayor and five councillors 
from a slate of more than two dozen candidates - including the ex-mayor and councillors who were fired by the 
province last year.
The much-anticipated vote was triggered by the Alberta government's rare decision to boot the city's then-mayor 
Jeff Colvin( https://calgaryherald.com/news/local-news/province-fires-chestermere-mayor-three-councillors-spared 
), councillors Mel Foat, Blaine Funk and Stephen Hanley, and three top city officials last December. Municipal 
Affairs Minister Ric McIver said at the time council had failed to quell dysfunction identified by a municipal 
inspection and didn't adhere to a province-installed supervisor or the binding directives it was handed as a result of 
that investigation.
All four men are now running to reclaim their respective positions.
""This is just a bit of a bizarre series of events,"" said Mount Royal University political scientist Lori Williams. ""And it's 
got to be frustrating for the people of Chestermere with all these questions swirling around and so many barriers to 
effective governance in their municipality.""
Three councillors, Sandy Johal-Watt, Shannon Dean and Ritesh Narayan, were spared by McIver's dismissal order, 
though Narayan is the only member of the last council with a confirmed spot on the new one. Johal-Watt resigned 
and took a job in city administration, while Dean stepped down to run for mayor.
Colvin and Dean are joined on the mayoral ballot( https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/fired-ex-mayor-
candidates-chestermere-byelection ) by Marshall Chalmers, another ex-Chestermere mayor, and former city 
councillor Christopher Steeves. Twenty-three candidates are running for the five open councillor seats.
New council to address financial inquiry findings
Williams said while Monday's vote could mark the end of turbulence within Chestermere's government, it ""isn't 
going to settle the issue."" The four ousted politicians are still pursuing legal action against the province's dismissal 
order and making numerous claims about bias, corruption and conspiracy being behind their dismissals.
""We are not going to hear the end of this; this is going to be an ongoing controversy for some time to come,"" said 
Williams.

""Both publicly and legally, I think this is going to continue - the allegations and the objections are going to continue. 
But, again, I think for the people of Chestermere, their primary concern is whether (candidates) will be able to 
govern effectively for the interests of their municipality.""
A piece of art is shown near the City of Chestermere main building in Chestermere, east of Calgary on Tuesday, 
May 28, 2024.
As directed by the province, one of the new mayor and council's first orders of business will be to formulate plans to 
address the 94 recommendations of a recent financial probe of the city. The Deloitte-led investigation - ordered by 
the province after the dismissals - found a laundry list of issues, including multiple expenditures made without 
proper council approval.
Last week, the city sued Colvin, Foat, Funk and Hanley for more than $650,000( 
https://calgaryherald.com/news/local-news/chestermere-sues-fired-mayor-councillors-650k ) - based partly on 
Deloitte's findings. The city claims the four improperly spent taxpayer dollars on lawyers to fight their dismissals, 
booze, and equipment to surveil city staff, among other costs.
The four have denied all of the allegations, and Colvin has said the lawsuit amounts to interference in the byelection 
by city officials.
The city's claims have not been tested in court.

counters( https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/smith-on-bill-20 ), meaning Monday night's tally will be done by 
hand, delaying unofficial results.
Returning officer Noshy Karbani said the count would likely end hours after polls close at 8 p.m. in the early 
morning hours of Tuesday, with a preliminary tally to be unveiled soon after. Each candidate will be allowed one 
person in the room - a person or scrutineer of their choosing or themselves.
""It would be ideal if we could have everything done by 1 a.m., 1:30 a.m. But that is if everything goes according to 
plan,"" Karbani told Postmedia last week.
Karbani said with Chestermere's population swelling to more than 25,000, voter turnout could be higher than the 
4,700 ballots cast in the 2021 election.
Almost 2,800 people voted in advanced polls between June 15 and June 17.
Residents will vote throughout the day at the Chestermere Recreation Centre.

Ottawa is still reeling from Thursday's bombshell allegation that then-defence minister Harjit Sajjan personally 
directed Canadian special forces to rescue more than 200 Afghan Sikhs during the fall of Kabul in August 2021. It 
was a directive, according to military sources quoted in the Globe and Mail, that diverted critical resources away 
from the evacuation of Canadian citizens, translators and other Afghans who'd aided Canada's twodecade-long 
war effort in the country.
And while the details of the report are indeed shocking, they're hardly surprising. Sajjan raised potential red flags 
from, quite literally, the day he was nominated and should have never been given the defence portfolio in the first 
place. What's more, Sajjan himself is a symptom of the Trudeau Liberals'borderline obsession with domestic 
diaspora politics.
Sajjan's family ties to the controversial World Sikh Organization were well known before he entered politics - so 
much so that his nomination as the Liberal candidate for Vancouver South in late 2014 prompted a number of 
moderate Sikhs in the riding to tear up their party memberships in protest.
One such objector warned at the time, ""The Liberal party, especially Justin (Trudeau), is in bed with extremist and 
fundamental groups."" This warning, and others like it, would regrettably go unheeded with an obsequious media 
seemingly more concerned with the young upstart's luscious locks and sock game.
The soon-to-be prime minister's sordid bet would nevertheless pay off over the short term. With Sajjan as the 
party's candidate, the upstart Liberals would easily flip the Conservative-held riding in the next year's federal 
election. Sajjan was, of course, subsequently elevated to the inner-cabinet post of defence as a rookie MP.
It didn't take long for controversy to follow Sajjan in his new role. He would notably be forced to apologize in 2017 
for a pattern of misleading statements he made embellishing his record of military service in Afghanistan. The 
apology came on the heels of Sajjan's disastrous diplomatic visit to India, wherein he was publicly snubbed by 
Punjab's top elected official over his alleged ties to Sikh separatists.
Sajjan would somehow manage to keep his job as defence minister for six years, despite garnering reviews that 
were middling at best throughout his turbulent tenure in the portfolio. In June 2021, just two months before the ill-
fated Afghanistan evacuation, he was censured by his colleagues in the House of Commons for his abysmal 
handling of rampant sexual misconduct in Canada's military.

By the summer of 2021, it was abundantly clear to anyone paying attention that Sajjan was unfit to be defence 
minister. No one should be surprised by the critical lack of judgment and ethics he allegedly showed amid the

And while Sajjan currently occupies a far less high-profile cabinet post, it still boggles the mind that a man who's

preparedness.
Why not put Captain Ahab in charge of the Fisheries Department while we're at it? While it would be easy to 
dismiss Sajjan as one bad apple, the truth is that he is a symptom of the Liberal party's deeply cynical approach to 
ethnic outreach - an inconvenient reality that has allowed the manipulation of our domestic politics by foreign actors 
to swell to epidemic proportions under Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's watch.

minister's fear of losing the ""Sikh vote"" to the NDP after Jagmeet Singh took the helm of the party in 2017. (Singh, 
coincidentally, chose to run for a seat in Greater Vancouver after winning the leadership race.)

Now, the federal government is taking kicks at Canada Soccer for its drone spying scandal.

suspended women's national team head coach Bev Priestman and staff members Joey Lombardi and Jasmine 
Mander for the one-year duration of their FIFA ban.
""Using a drone to surveil another team during a closed practice is cheating,"" Qualtrough said in a statement. ""It is 
completely unfair to Canadian players and to opposing teams. It undermines the integrity of the game itself.""
On Saturday, FIFA stripped Canada of six points in the group stage standings, banned the three coaches from all 
soccer activities for the next year and fined Canada Soccer the equivalent of $313,000.
""Given that the women's program receives funding from Sport Canada, we are withholding funding relating to 
suspended Canada Soccer officials for the duration of their FIFA sanction,"" Qualtrough said in the statement. 
""There is a deeply concerning pattern of behaviour at Canada Soccer. We must, and will, get to the bottom of this.""
The minister's office later clarified in an email to Postmedia how the change in funding will impact the Canada 
Soccer program.
""Sport Canada is in the process of determining the exact amount of funding to be withheld. It will be specific to 
suspended Canada Soccer officials and not impact the overall available funding to the Women's Program,"" a 
representative from the minister's office said in an email.
""At this time, I can confirm that that funding is allocation for salary.""
She expects the federal government to closely monitor Canada Soccer's external investigation and outcomes of the 
process that is underway. The Future of Sport in Canada commission will also make recommendations to the 
government on improvements in the country's sport system.
""This issue has caused significant distraction and embarrassment for Team Canada and all Canadians here in 
Paris and at home,"" Qualtrough said. ""It is deeply regrettable.""

EDMONTON A Law Society of Alberta tribunal committee is considering whether to sanction former Alberta justice 
minister Kaycee Madu for placing a phone call to Edmonton's police chief shortly after receiving a distracted 
driving ticket.
Last July, the law society cited Madu, alleging he undermined respect for the administration of justice through his 
March 2021 call to Edmonton Police Services Chief Dale McFee, which came soon after the traffic stop.
On Wednesday, a three-day hearing into the incident concluded with the three-person tribunal committee reserving 
its decision, stating a written ruling will come ""in due course.""
'POLITICAL AND MEDIA STORM'
Law society lawyer Ken McEwan was first to give closing arguments.
He stated Madu using his position as justice minister to raise the ticket privately with the police chief produced a 
perception of interference, arguing the minister ""had no objective basis"" to make the call.
""What would a reasonable member of the public think about that? Would their respect for the administration of 
justice in Alberta be encouraged or undermined?""
He further argued Madu had acted without integrity or regard for
the consequences of his conduct.
""Taking the facts in the best possible light, in making the phone call to Chief McFee he acted without regard to the 
potential harm to the public perception of the administration of justice.""
Madu's lawyer, Perry Mack, asked the committee to look past ""the political and media storm"" around the incident 
and to consider Madu's work at the time on the issue of carding and what were then recent revelations about 
members of the Lethbridge police surveilling an MLA.

Much of that work, Mack stated, involved frequent direct contact with police chiefs.
""He is absolutely entitled to pick up his cellphone and call the chief of police at any time about carding or racial 
profiling, whatever the trigger,"" he said. ""The ticket may well have been the prompt. So what?"" He cautioned 
against assuming Madu's motivation for the call, arguing there was no evidence he was seeking a personal benefit.
""If we are going to judge Mr.
Madu's thoughts, motivations and actions ... they must be judged through the standard of a Black man, a Black 
minister of justice, a person who has spent six months getting an earful from the Black and ethnic communities 
about policing.""
Both Madu and the officer who pulled him over, Edmonton police Const. Ryan Brooks, testified that the issue of 
race did not play a role in the stop.

given Tuesday by Brooks, whose notes indicated Madu referenced his title as justice minister on four occasions

In a recent podcast, senior Conservative strategist Fred DeLorey said that the 2019 blackface scandal actually 
caused Prime Minister Justin Trudeau to win re-election.
""I think that issue actually got him re-elected because Conservatives just went on that like a dog on a bone. They 
dropped all their messaging on affordability and the economy and they focused on blackface,"" DeLorey said in a 
May 27 episode of his podcast On Background.
The occasion was an interview with political journalist Stephen Maher, whose new book The Prince contains the 
most detailed account to date of how the Liberal campaign reacted to the scandal. On Sept. 19, 2019 - just eight 
days after the writ had been dropped for the 43rd federal election - Time magazine published photos showing 
Trudeau wearing brownface at an Arabian Nights-themed party at West Point Grey Academy, the Vancouver 
private high school where Trudeau worked as a teacher.
This spawned the release of multiple other photos showing Trudeau wearing full-body ethnic makeup at points 
throughout his 20s, including one time where he wore blackface to perform an impression of singer Harry Belafonte.
Maher's book includes the detail that Trudeau had told his advisers that all these photos existed, but they had 
simply carried on with the hope that they would never be published.
Maher's own take on the scandal, as written in The Prince, is that if they had come out in the 2015 election they 
would have scotched
Trudeau's chances of ever becoming prime minister in the first place.
""They would have reinforced the Conservative message about Trudeau and raised doubts within his multicultural 
progressive coalition,"" wrote Maher.
But when they came up in 2019, DeLorey's view was that they caused Conservatives to lean on the notion that 
Trudeau was a racist, when most voters were more inclined to the view that he was just an idiot.
""They tried to make the ballot question, 'Is Justin Trudeau racist or not?' He's not. No one believes that.
And we lost our message track."" DeLorey told Maher. ""Yes, he was a dumb kid, but it doesn't mean he was racist.""

According to the polls, however, the Conservatives were always the underdog in the 2019 election, and the 
blackface scandal did surprisingly little to alter Canadian voting intentions. A Sept. 17 L eger poll issued on the eve 
of the blackface photos being made public showed the Liberals polling at 34 per cent to the Conservatives' 33 per 
cent.
Two weeks later - after images of Trudeau in blackface had exploded around the world - another Leger poll 
delivered the near-identical result of having the Liberals and Conservatives tied at 34 per cent.
And both Leger polls were right on target with the final voting results. In terms of popular vote, the Conservatives 
received 34.34 per cent of ballots to the Liberals' 33.12 per cent.
Despite this plurality in votes, the Conservatives won just 121 seats to the Liberals' 157.
The gap was explained by what Liberal strategists would later term ""vote efficiency"": The Liberals were able to win

DeL ore y, now an Ottawa-based PR consultant, was a Conservative organizer as far back as 2004, when he 
spearheaded Stephen Harper's successful leadership bid. DeLorey was an unsuccessful Tory candidate in Peter 
MacKay's old riding of Central Nova, N.S., in 2015, and in the 2021 federal election would be the Conservatives' 
national campaign director.

Conservative perspective on the issue.

The New York jury's unanimous verdict convicting Donald Trump on 34 felony counts, essentially for falsifying 
business records in violation of campaign finance regulations, injects more uncertainty into the 2024 presidential 
election. For Democrats - and particularly Trump-haters - the reaction was ecstatic. Some stated fervently that the 
rule of law and the principle that no one is above the law were upheld. In a highly polarized America, many strongly 
dissented. For diehard Trump supporters, the verdict was ""rigged,"" a ""sham"" and an example of how the legal 
system has been ""politicized"" against them. Trump's campaign attracted US$50 million in donations within 48 hours 
of the verdict.
Early polls indicated that 57 per cent of Americans regarded the verdict as ""fair,"" though there was little sign that the 
intricacies of the trial were followed attentively. As Bloomberg editorialized, ""Whatever one's view of the verdict, 
these are incredibly grim signs for American politics.""
Sentencing is scheduled for July 11, just four days before the Republican convention. Because of his age, and 
because he is a first-time offender, it is unlikely Trump will receive a prison sentence. Probation and/or fines are 
more likely, but no one knows what restrictions a probationary sentence could have on his campaign efforts.
Trump certainly intends to appeal the verdict, but it is doubtful his appeals will be concluded before the Nov. 5 
election, when the American public will register, according to Trump, the ""only"" verdict that counts. His supporters 
claim he has many grounds for appeal:
? The district attorney, Alvin Bragg, ran on a campaign promising to ""get"" Trump.
? The presiding judge, Juan Merchan, ruled for the prosecutor many times while ignoring several pleas from 
Trump's defence team.
? Judge Merchan's convoluted instructions to the jury signalled the verdict he wanted, as did his acceptance of the 
D.A.'s linkage of a lapsed state misdemeanour to a federal campaign finance felony as the basis for all charges on 
which Trump was convicted.
? ""Hush money"" was never a legal issue.
Trump may not have been wellserved by his legal team but his tempestuous nature and penchant for publicity 
made him a difficult client to represent. He breached the gag order imposed on him by the judge and was fined 10 
times during the trial.
Page 2 of 3
Verdict's out on U.S. election fallout; Legal woes Bedevil Trump, Biden
Now Trump has a criminal record - a historical first for a former U.S. president. Technically, as a convicted felon, he 
is unable to travel to countries like Canada. Voters cannot reverse the New York court's convictions, but they could 
effectively nullify them politically by returning Trump to the White House regardless of his felonies, and those that 
may still follow.
Trump has other legal woes pending over his handling of classified documents and his role in the Jan. 6, 2021 riots 
on Capitol Hill, both of which are already delayed beyond the election. His immunity appeal to the Supreme Court 
should be resolved soon but, at best, he may receive partial, not complete immunity.
Legal troubles are also afflicting Trump's opponent for re-election. Just last week President Joe Biden's son, 
Hunter, was convicted on three felony charges relating to his lying on a gun licence application. President Biden 
said he ""will accept the outcome of this case and will continue to respect the judicial process as Hunter considers 
an appeal."" In September, Hunter faces further felony charges in California for tax evasion. If nothing else, his 
Delaware conviction should help temper complaints about a ""politicized"" legal system.
While the Trump and Biden verdicts dominated the news in the week following each, they may have less staying 
power during the campaign. At this juncture no one really knows. Polls consistently show that Americans are more 
concerned about inflation and the economy, immigration and the border crisis.
The first debate on June 27 will give an early read on the election implications of Trump's conviction. Pollsters 
contend that the group most likely to be swayed will be the 20 to 25 per cent who favour neither Trump nor Biden. 
Even more determinate will be the effect on voters in key battleground states like Michigan, Wisconsin, 
Pennsylvania, North Carolina, Georgia, Arizona and Nevada.
There are serious concerns about whether either candidate is ""fit"" to be president - Biden's mental acuity versus 
Trump's unpredictable temperament, as well as his conviction.
The challenge for Biden is to demonstrate more convincingly to voters that he is fighting for them, whereas Trump is 
fighting for himself. The challenge for Trump will be to resist playing the ""victim"" card and celebrate his record in 
office versus that of Biden, along with ideas on what he will do as president.
Kitchen-table issues play to Trump's advantage. Biden keeps switching his economic message, but none has really 
resonated. Belatedly using executive action to check illegal migrants at the border may help but could be too little, 
too late.
Additionally, there are looming questions about the competence of Biden's administration. The US$320-million 
temporary pier that the U.S. military built offshore in Gaza to facilitate humanitarian assistance has twice broken 
apart in rough seas, with some portions becoming beached and others floating away and starting to sink, and the 
pier may now be temporarily dismantled for repair yet again. That is, of course, not the president's fault, but he is 
responsible for the actions of his administration.
The penchant for micromanaging Israel and Ukraine's military tactics is proving to be counterproductive. Biden and 
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are publicly at loggerheads over Israel's attacks in Gaza. On Memorial 
Day weekend, The New York Times reported that some American-made, precision-guided weapons supplied to 
Ukraine had proven ineffective on the battlefield due to electronic jamming by Russia. Worse still, the U.S. had 
insisted Ukraine not hit targets inside Russia, including sites from which devastating attacks were launched on 
civilian infrastructure in the besieged city of Kharkiv. The U.S. eventually reversed partially this limitation, as it had 
done on earlier reversals.
Confidence in U.S. institutions is ebbing, and increasing signs of global turmoil exacerbate matters. Concerns about 
competence and character are why many Americans wish they had different choices for president.

Toronto MP and former public safety minister Marco Mendicino was spat on by a protester in Ottawa this week, a 
video circulating online appears to show.
Mendicino confirmed an incident occurred on Wednesday, the day the House of Commons adjourned for the 
summer, in an email to the Star.
""I will not be commenting given that the incident is under investigation,"" he said. ""It is not the first time. I've been 
the target of multiple death threats and incidents of harassment.""
The video, which has been viewed thousands of times on YouTube and Reddit, shows a man wearing a ""Save 
Canada"" hat approaching Mendicino on Sparks Street near Parliament Hill and spitting on him as Mendicino 
reached out to shake his hand. The man later apologizes to Mendicino.
Save Canada, an organization that gained prominence during the so-called ""Freedom Convoy"" in 2022, says on its 
Facebook page that it promotes ""the Free Christian Values, culture and History of Canada.""
The incident comes as Canadian elected officials of all political stripes face an unprecedented surge in physical 
threats and intimidation, the Star has reported. That has extended beyond online threats and includes garages 
being set on fire and windows being smashed.
Liberal MP Pam Damoff, who represents an Oakville riding, told the Star last month she was not seeking re-election 
in part because of the ""threats and misogyny"" she has faced.
In this instance, the video shows Mendicino being confronted by a small group of protesters, one of whom has a ""F 
- Trudeau"" flag on his back.
As Mendicino enters the Valour Building, where some MPs have offices, he stops to reach out to shake one 
protestor's hand. The video shows the man spitting in Mendicino's face.
""That doesn't seem very nice,"" the MP for Toronto's Eglinton-Lawrence riding says as he retreats into the building.
""You're a disgrace,"" an unidentified voice yells. ""You're a parasite,"" another voice chimes in.

The protesters then walk away, before a Parliamentary Protective Service officer comes out with Mendocino, who 
points at them.
""I'm just sick and tired of these people now walking around here like they own God,"" the video captures an unseen 
person saying.
The video shows the officer approaching the man and asking him to apologize.
The man walks back to the building, apologizes to Mendicino, and they shake hands.
""I'm sorry, OK?"" the man says. ""I'm just frustrated. I just don't like our prime minister.""
The video was posted to YouTube by ""Canadian Free Living,"" an anti-government account that frequently 
documents confrontations around Parliament Hill.
Save Canada did not respond to an email seeking comment on Friday afternoon.
In a statement to the Star, an Ottawa Police Service spokesperson said there were ""no calls for service on Sparks 
Street this week related to such a matter.""
They also said ""it is possible that the Ottawa Police Service is not the police of jurisdiction in the matter.""
The Parliamentary Protective Service did not respond to a request for comment on Friday afternoon.
However, the question of jurisdiction, or which police force is responsible for enforcing the law on streets just off 
Parliament Hill, has been clear since the Freedom Convoy jammed downtown Ottawa for weeks in 2022.
A security source, speaking on background, said the Ottawa Police Service still is the police service of jurisdiction 
for everything outside the fence that surrounds Parliament Hill's major buildings, the Peace Tower, and West and 
East Blocks.
The federal government has been in talks with the City of Ottawa to extend the formal parliamentary precinct 
boundaries to give the Parliamentary Protective Service - which is headed by the RCMP - jurisdiction, but those 
negotiations have not concluded.
In the interim, the federal government has given Ottawa police $50 million over five years to establish a dedicated 
unit to policing the area. However, it is rare that officers are seen patrolling there, except for when organized 
protests are scheduled.

Politics doesn't have to be the cruellest game, but that's usually the way it is played. Right now, for instance, Deputy 
Prime Minister Chrystia Freeland is definitely being played.
Three weeks ago, the political pressure was on Prime Minister Justin Trudeau. Would he quit after the Liberals lost 
the ultrasafe seat of Toronto-St. Paul's? Former Liberal ministers openly called for new leadership as did one 
current backbencher, Wayne Long.
What is needed in these circumstances is a distraction to take the heat off the prime minister. And nothing says 
distraction better than the possibility of a minister - the deputy prime minister, say - being thrown under a bus (a 
note for the unimaginative: that's a figure of speech and not a call for homicide by public transport.)
Earlier this month, the Globe and Mail reported that within the Prime Minister's Office (PMO), there were worries 
that Freeland was not selling the government's economic policies as well as she should. Trudeau had also 
acknowledged courting former Bank of Canada governor Mark Carney to get him to join the government.
The implications were clear: Freeland was on the way out and Carney on the way in.
However, such feverish and uninformed speculation must have been laid to rest last week when the prime minister 
gave Freeland a full-throated endorsement: ""I have full confidence in her abilities, and the work we're going to be 
doing together,"" he said.
Indeed, when rumours swirled in August 2020 about the fate of the last finance minister, Bill Morneau, Trudeau 
was equally assured in his conviction.
""The prime minister has full confidence in Minister Morneau and any statement to the contrary is false,"" Trudeau's 
communications director said at the time. Less than a week later, Morneau resigned because of irreconcilable 
differences with Trudeau. A coincidence? Perhaps. In February 2019, as the SNC-Lavalin scandal reared its head 
and questions were raised about the integrity and ethics of the prime minister, Trudeau gave a strong backing to 
Jody Wilson-Raybould, then the veterans affairs minister and formerly the attorney general.
""I continue to have full confidence in Jody,"" he told a press conference. Wilson-Raybould quit the next day. It is 
tempting to cite ""irreconcilable differences"" again, but that might not be an accurate description of their relationship, 
since, according to her book, Indian in the Cabinet, Wilson-Raybould once told Trudeau, ""I wish that I had never 
met you.""
Page 2 of 3
Watch for that knife, Chrystia Freeland; Let Bill Morneau's fate be a lesson
When Trudeau expresses full confidence in a minister, rest assured the PMO is checking the bus timetables. One 
of the problems when the Liberals do this sort of backstabbing - call it the night of the long knives, the short knives 
or the kitchen knives, whatever - is that it detracts from their ability to govern. Policies, new directives and important 
government announcements are all ignored as the prime minister grapples with the optics of a given situation. It is 
one of the things Morneau complained about in his book about his time in government, Where To From Here: A 
Path to Canadian Prosperity.
""Policy rationales were tossed aside in favour of scoring political points,"" he wrote, adding that recommendations 
from the finance ministry were ignored ""in favour of winning a popularity contest."" Marc Garneau, former minister of 
foreign affairs and transport, tells a similar tale in his upcoming autobiography, A Most Extraordinary Ride: Space, 
Politics and the Pursuit of a Canadian Dream, slated for release in October. The government was too reactive, he 
says. ""It is not sufficient to pay attention only when a concern arises, something this government has made a habit 
of,"" writes Garneau, who said he was ""blindsided"" when he was dropped as foreign affairs minister after 10 
months.
Both men have noted Trudeau's distant relationship with his cabinet. Morneau said Trudeau ""had an inability, or 
lack of interest, in forging relationships with me, and as far as I could tell, with the rest of his cabinet."" Garneau 
references the prime minister's ""aloofness."" Maybe Trudeau has problems forming attachments with people who 
are intellectually, and educationally, superior.
Does he feel threatened by the Harvard- and Oxford-educated Freeland? Morneau and Garneau were very capable 
ministers, but that didn't matter. Once Trudeau had tired of them, or once scapegoats were needed, they were out. 
Freeland has been loyal to Trudeau, but she serves at the pleasure of the prime minister.
When he is displeased, careers tend to implode. On Tuesday, Freeland was in Markham, Ont., talking about low-
carbon energy networks, but the press conference was dominated by questions about whether she still had a future 
as finance minister and deputy prime minister. Had Trudeau raised concerns about her, she was asked. Better 
ask the prime minister, she replied.
Pushed again, she replied, ""To serve as minister in a cabinet, you do need the support and confidence of the 
prime minister. ... I do have to feel that I have that confidence."" There we have it, Freeland is confident that she 
has the confidence of the prime minister. Meanwhile, the No. 32 to Parliament Hill will be along any moment.

Ethics Commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein is taking another look at concerns Employment Minister Randy 
Boissonnault stayed in touch with his former company after being appointed to cabinet.
Parliament's ethics committee has been studying whether Boissonnault was an active participant in the medical 
supply business he co-owned after he was appointed to cabinet, which would have violated ethics rules.
The issue first came to light through a Global News story centred on text messages between Stephen Anderson, 
who co-founded Global Health Imports (GHI) with Boissonnault, and a client.
The text message referred to someone named Randy asking for a ""partner call."" It was sent on Sept. 8, 2022, a 
year after Boissonnault said he resigned from the company.
Boissonnault was tourism minister at the time.
Cabinet ministers are banned by ethics laws from operating or managing businesses while in office.

Give credit where credit is due. Wales has given the world many fine and useful firsts. Ball bearings, tennis and the 
microphone have been attributed to Welsh initiative.
A group of Welsh men from the town of Merthyr Tydfil once took part in a medical study of a drug to treat angina 
and reported a hard-to-hide side-effect. We have those weak-hearted men to thank for Viagra.
And now, in the final days of the United Kingdom's election campaign, the territory on England's western border that 
is home to just over three million people could be poised to put the great back in Great Britain.
This, after the Welsh government announced Tuesday it would introduce legislation making it a criminal offence for 
politicians to lie to Parliament.
Like many political breakthroughs, the pledge by the Welsh Labour government was the result of an ultimatum 
made by opposition parties, the BBC reported. Do it or face defeat.
The motion passed by a vote of 26-13, with 13 members of the Welsh parliament, the Senedd, abstaining. 
The government promised to pass legislation before the next scheduled election in 2026.
It's been a labour of many years for the architect and main mover of the initiative, Adam Price.
In 2007, the member of the U.K. Parliament led the charge to have then-prime minister Tony Blair sanctioned over 
the country's participation in the 2003 U.S.-led invasion of Iraq.
Price was ejected from the House of Commons in 2005 for alleging that Blair ""misled"" Parliament.
A later inquiry ruled the Blair government had exaggerated the threat posed by Iraqi president Saddam Hussein and 
that ""the judgments about Iraq's capabilities ... were presented with a certainty that was not justified.""
Price left the U.K. parliament in 2010, but returned six years later to the Welsh legislature, still fixated on what could 
well serve as his signature contribution to political life.
""It's a very, very simple but central principle, really,"" he said during a recent debate on the matter in the Senedd. 
""That deliberate deception in politics should never been acceptable.""
Page 2 of 3
Would a Welsh law put end to lying politicians?
He noted that lawyers can be disbarred for lying in court, fibbing physicians can lose their licence, dishonest 
company directors risk shareholder revolts and even businesses are legally prevented from making dishonest 
claims about their products.
""The bizarre situation,"" he said, ""is that there are more consequences for calling people a liar than actually being a 
liar.""
In an age of Donald Trump, of disinformation, of foreign interference and extremist political positions, it's possible 
that truer words have never been spoken.
In Canada's House of Commons, the Speaker is all-too-often called upon to police unbecoming parliamentary 
language, without addressing the founding basis for claims made by politicians in the legislature.
The tradition of parliamentary privilege allows MPs great leeway in the arguments they make, but tightly restricts 
other members' ability to call them out for errors, intentional or otherwise.
In May, Conservative MP Rick Perkins tried to get around the prohibition on calling someone a ""liar"" in the 
Commons by referring to NDP MP Peter Julian as an ""unmitigated falsifier of veracity.""
Last December, Conservative MP Damien Kurek was kicked out of the Commons for accusing Prime Minister 
Justin Trudeau of giving orders to senators to amend a bill that would give some farmers an exemption from parts 
of the federal carbon tax.
This occurred, Kurek said, despite Trudeau's claims that Senators acted independently of his Liberal government.
""The prime minister himself was on the phone over the weekend, telling them they had to gut Bill C-234,"" he 
charged. ""The prime minister lied, and his minions continue to lie ...""
Asked to withdraw his comments, Kurek refused and was booted from the legislature.
Other jurisdictions have, in fact, taken action against lying politicians, though the matters have been more 
substantial than partisan quibbles.
In February, former Austrian chancellor Sebastian Kurz was convicted of charges that he had given false evidence 
to a parliamentary investigative committee.
And this week, South Australia MP Fraser Ellis was found guilty of ""deception"" - a criminal charge comparable to 
fraud - in a case involving the misuse of his official travel expense and accommodation allowance.
The Welsh legislation might not put an end to corruption and fraud, just as criminal charges for theft, murder and 
espionage have yet to rid the world of stealing, killing and spying, and just as international humanitarian law has not 
brought war crimes to an end.
But it might cause lying legislators to clean up their act, or at least force public officials to think twice before trying to 
pull the wool over the eyes of their electors.
Of course, that is if - and only if - the Welsh government follows through on what it has promised.

A Mexican businessman and lawyer accused of aiding imprisoned former Veracruz governor Javier Duarte has won 
another chance at refugee status in Canada.
Moises Mansur Cysneiros recently won a Federal Court of Canada application to have his case reviewed again by 
the Immigration and Refugee Board's appeal division after earlier attempts to get refugee status were denied.
Judge Janet Fuhrer said the Refugee Appeal Division failed to fully consider the possibility that an RCMP warning 
to Mansur in 2017 about threats to his family might have been linked to political opponents in Mexico.
Mansur originally applied for refugee status in Canada six years ago, arguing that he faced persecution in his home 
country because of his long-time friendship with Duarte that dated back to when both men were in law school.
But the federal public safety minister asserted at two earlier hearings that Mansur was not eligible to remain in 
Canada because of allegations of tax fraud, organized crime and money laundering against him in Mexico that 
stemmed from the investigation into Duarte.
Duarte was convicted of money laundering and having criminal associations and sentenced in 2018 to nine years in 
jail.
Mansur asserted that Duarte's political opponents, including Miguel Angel Yunes - who succeeded Duarte as 
governor - targeted him after he arrived in Canada. Yunes even travelled to meet Mansur in Toronto in 2016, urging 
Mansur to help implicate Duarte, the refugee board heard.
The RCMP visited Mansur's Vancouver house in February 2017 and told him about the threat to himself and his 
family, although no more details were provided.
The appeal division panel ruled that any link between the 2017 threat and rival politicians was ""speculative.""
But Fuhrer said that finding was in error, given that the panel accepted evidence that Yunes had in fact travelled to 
Canada to meet with Mansur seeking incriminating information about Duarte.
The meeting was secretly recorded by Yunes and parts were later broadcast on a Mexican TV news show.

American Iron & Metal is asking a judge to cancel the province's suspension of operations at its west Saint John 
scrapyard, saying it was done unreasonably in the wake of a massive fire Sept. 14. 
AIM filed an application Monday in Saint John Court of Kings Bench. In the legal filing, the company asked for an 
order quashing the suspension as well as handing over any records or evidence used in the decision. 
In the days after the fire at the Gateway Street scrapyard, which is leased from Port Saint John, the province 
suspended the recycling firm's approval to operate, citing ""an unauthorized release of contaminants,"" contrary to 
the Clean Air Act. 
In December, a task force assembled by the province and Port Saint John found scrap metal piles at the facility 
were at least twice as high as allowed by the national fire code, and that AIM's operations are an ""environmental, 
health and safety risk to Saint John."" 
The fire started just after 1 a.m. on Sept. 14 in a scrap metal pile 12 to 15 metres high and was brought under 
control more than a day later. In an affidavit, AIM's Vice President, Eastern Region Michael Cormier said that 
despite media comments from Premier Blaine Higgs on Sept. 14 that operations would be suspended pending an 
investigation, and a Sept. 18 press release announcing the formation of the task force, the province never formally 
suspended its operating approval until Sept. 19 
""I was again, surprised when I read the news release because AIM had not been informed that its approval had 
been suspended,"" Cormier wrote. 
AIM argues in the application that the letter from Environment and Local Government Minister Gary Crossman 
lacked ""adequate information"" on the contaminant allegedly released and ""arbitrarily and unreasonably"" suspended 
its approval indefinitely, without conditions that AIM could fulfil to restore the approval, and that it's prevented from 
operating its business until the approval is listed. 
According to the affidavit, which spans more than 800 pages including emails and consultant reports, AIM 
unsuccessfully appealed the decision to suspend the approval to Crossman. The minister gave interim approval to 
AIM to carry out remedial work and an environmental impact assessment on the site, as well as cleaning and 
monitoring tasks, conditional on approval from Port Saint John.

Cormier said that AIM has submitted a remediation action plan and is ""prepared to mobilize,"" but ""continues to 
suffer significant economic damages"" because of the suspension. The approval to operate expires in April. 
AIM's application argues that the suspension is unreasonable and arbitrary because Crossman failed to justify why 
the suspension was necessary ""and why no lesser penalty would have sufficed,"" as well as ""relying excessively"" on 
the investigation of the task force. 
Cormier cited five incidents at the Irving Oil refinery, from 1988 to the 2018 explosion, where he said there was no 
shutdown after the matter was resolved, and said there was no further regulatory action taken following a tire fire in 
Minto in 2019. 
The task force found that the environmental impact assessment – as part of AIM's approval to operate an industrial 
shredder in 2011 – failed to consider explosions and fire, saying there had been 181 explosions and 22 fires since 
2011, as well as 21 WorkSafe NB incident investigations, with two fatalities. 
In Cormier's affidavit, he said AIM and Port Saint John battled over its investigation, with AIM suggesting that Port 
Saint John was in a conflict of interest position as the landowner and as investigator through the task force. 
AIM denied Port Saint John access to interviewing its employees, and answered a list of 43 questions in writing, 
Cormier said in the affidavit. 
Cormier said in his affidavit that the province only initially provided the task force's report and five related consultant 
reports when it made a Right to Information request to four departments for all information and documents 
regarding AIM since Jan. 1, 2023. The province has since said it's still working on the request, according to the 
filing. 
The company said Port Saint John denied a similar RTI request, with an email from Port Saint John saying the 
request was ""overly broad."" AIM also said it has submitted RTI requests on the five Irving Oil incidents as well as 
the Minto tire fire. 
In December, Public Safety Minister Kris Austin revoked the site's salvage dealer's licence, which AIM can apply to 
be judicially reviewed. This decision is not mentioned in the court filing. 
Department of the environment spokesperson Clarissa Andersen and Port Saint John's external affairs manager 
Patrick Beamish both declined comment, citing that the matter is before the court. Brunswick News did not receive 
a response to a request for comment from AIM by press time.

The federal auditor general has asked police to investigate two fired employees who had undeclared contracts with 
the government.
In a statement to National Post, the Office of the Auditor General (OAG) said it is still investigating a third employee 
it also discovered had contracts with another federal government organization they had not disclosed.
The firings, which occurred between September and December last year, come to light as questions swirl about 
how another federal public servant's company was able to obtain a nearly $8-million contract to work on the 
ArriveCan app.
It also shows that no federal organization - including the biggest watchdog of government contracting which recently 
published a scathing report on ArriveCan - is immune from employees breaking their code of conduct and 
potentially the law by failing to report all secondary employment.
York University assistant professor and ethics expert Ian Stedman said it's time for the government to start being 
more proactive in checking if public servants are respecting their values and ethics code as opposed to relying on 
attestations signed by each bureaucrat.
For example, he said each department and agency could have a team whose job is to randomly pick certain public 
servants to be ""audited,"" which could include a review of their expense reports and verifying that they don't have 
undeclared secondary sources of income.
""Because our work dynamics and our work cultures have shifted so much (since the pandemic), we probably have 
to have a layer of oversight and auditing enforcement to kind of continue to reinforce that the rules matter, and that 
they have consequences,"" Stedman said.
Testifying as part of the House Public Accounts committee's study on the ArriveCan controversy, Auditor General 
Karen Hogan said last week her office had not detected that the president and CEO of Dalian, which received $7.9 
million in contracts for ArriveCan, now worked for the Department of National Defence because the latter was not 
part of the audit.
She noted that it is ""essential"" for public servants to disclose any secondary source of income to their managers so 
they can assess whether there is a conflict of interest, but that doesn't always happen.

That's when she first revealed that her office had recently discovered ""incidents where disclosure did not happen"" 
among its own employees.
In a series of detailed statements to National Post, OAG spokesperson Natasha Leduc said the office recently 
discovered that three of its employees had undeclared contracts with the Government of Canada. Two have since 
been fired while the third is still under internal investigation.
Leduc said the OAG first discovered the two fired employees had government contracts in June 2023 from Public 
Services and Procurement Canada (PSPC).
In one case, it was when PSPC asked the OAG if the employee of a company it was investigating still worked for 
the auditor general.
The OAG became suspicious of a second, newly hired employee when PSPC did not transfer the individual's 
security clearance because it had been suspended.
""The OAG conducted its own investigations in both cases. The investigations began in June 2023 and concluded in 
September in one case and December in the other. Based on the results of the investigations, the OAG revoked the 
individual's security clearance and terminated employment,"" Leduc said.
She said both cases were also referred to the Ottawa Police Service in early February because government 
directives dictate that ""security events that could potentially be related to criminal activity be referred to law 
enforcement.""
In light of those cases, Leduc said the OAG was implementing additional controls to verify outside employment or 
contracts and rolling out additional values and ethics training to all its employees.
Speaking to committee last week, PSPC deputy minister Arianne Reza said last week five department employees 
who did not disclose conflicts of interest were fired or resigned in the past year.

one case in September and the other in December.

Supreme Court in June 2023 where it seeks to have all the assets forfeited as proceeds of unlawful activity.
The B.C. NDP government introduced new measures last year to combat money laundering that include the 
unexplained wealth orders. If successful in court, the orders put a reverse onus on a person to explain where 
money came from to buy their assets in cases where there is suspicion of a crime.
""Gold bars may be highly liquid, and flashy luxury goods, such as jewelry and Rolex watches, attract attention, but

Sean McLeod will be something new to Alberta - an ethics commissioner who worked for the very government that 
now asks him to judge their behaviour.
McLeod was a deputy labour relations minister until last June, and since then has consulted with the deputy 
minister of executive council - the administrative boss of the whole government.
That's very close to the heart of political power.
For his toil as commissioner, McLeod will earn somewhere between $220,000 and $295,000 per year.
A lawyer who is First Nations, McLeod is clearly a substantial fellow. Deputy ministers can shock you with 
brilliance that isn't always obvious in the politicians who employ them.
The criticism his appointment faces may even make him eager to be fair and non-partisan.
But we're entitled to ask that existential question - what the hell?
Does Premier Danielle Smith even care about the impression the government makes?
This is a huge break with tradition.
Since the ethics office was created in 1992, there have been four commissioners before McLeod.
None of them had any formal connections with the government in power. The first one, Don Hamilton, had worked 
for Harry Strom, the final Socred premier.
Hamilton's successor, Bob Clark, had been a Socred minister and then party leader in the movement's dying 
days. His job was to oppose the PCs.
The Progressive Conservative majorities of those days still selected them.
Those men, both departed now, were hardly antagonistic to the PCs but at least had some genuine claim to 
independence.
